title: What the media is saying about the Cardinals inking WR Michael Wilson’s extension
summary: Arizona Cardinals’ GM Monti Ossenfort did this new offense a huge favor: He did not drag out receiver Michael Wilson’s contract extension. This was expected, but at what point in the season? Most GMs wait until December to determine what a player is worth. But that can backfire very easily. If the player has an […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - JANUARY 04: Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Michael Wilson #14 following his touchdown in the second half of an NFL game between the Arizona Cardinals and the Los Angeles Rams on January 4, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Arizona Cardinals’ GM Monti Ossenfort did this new offense a huge favor: He did not drag out receiver Michael Wilson’s contract extension. Cardinals reached agreement Wednesday with standout WR Michael Wilson on a three-year extension that keeps him in Arizona through the 2029 season, per me and @RapSheet . Wilson is expected to sign the deal today. pic.twitter.com/KFwk7GqC0L — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 3, 2026 This was expected, but at what point in the season? Most GMs wait until December to determine what a player is worth. But that can backfire very easily. If the player has an incredible season after 10-12 games, his value rises quite a bit. The flip side is that GMs assume that some players will lay off after getting bank and not have to play all out at an elite level simply because they got their money already. RELATED: CARDINALS AND WILSON AGREE TO 3-YEAR EXTENSION But most of the fanbase, the media, and this new Cardinals coaching staff have found out one thing about Wilson: He would play for free. He isn’t going to do less. He isn’t going to take plays off. It is very apparent that he loves the game, and he is happy with playing this game in the desert. Wilson doesn’t need tape to show his next team. He is with the team he loves. Wilson signed his extension in Tempe in front of his daughter Gigi and mother, Ngaire. His wife, Sophia, was in Portland for a game with the Portland Thorns of the National Women’s Soccer League. Wilson is now under contract through the 2029 season. When the franchise drafted Marv Harrison (6’-3”, 220 pounds) with the fourth pick in the 2024 NFL draft, the thought process was that the team would gravitate around their shiny new toy. But that hasn’t happened. Wilson (6’-2”, 213 pounds) came to Arizona as the #31 selection in Round 3 of the 2023 NFL draft. Earlier, they took OT Paris Johnson, DE B.J. Ojulari, and CB Garrett Williams. His ascension began last season because of two separate injuries. Harrison, nicknamed “Maserati Marv” in college, was the undisputed #1 receiver before he suffered a concussion, had an appendectomy in November, then suffered a heel injury in Week 13 and a foot injury in Week 17. Meanwhile, the Cardinals offense was manned by QB Kyler Murray. In Week 5, he suffered a foot injury against the winless Tennessee Titans and then was ruled out for the next three games. On November 5, the franchise placed Murray on IR. During the time Murray was the starting QB, Wilson’s stats were as follows: Week 1 (Saints) – Targets: 4, receptions: 1, yards: 5, touchdowns: 0, yards per catch average: 5.0 Week 2 (Panthers) – Targets: 2, receptions: 1, yards: 11, touchdowns: 1, yards per catch average: 11.0 Week 3 (49ers) – Targets: 2, receptions: 1, yards: 5, touchdowns: 0, yards per catch average: 5.0 Week 4 (Seahawks) – Targets: 6, receptions: 3, yards: 15, touchdowns: 0, yards per catch average: 5.0 Week 5 (Titans) – Targets: 4, receptions: 2, yards: 16, touchdowns: 0, yards per catch average: 8.0 When veteran backup Jacoby Brissett took over in Week 6, he found a friend in Wilson and TE Trey McBride. Brissett was more patient in the pocket than Murray, who would dart from the protection quickly, then look to throw or flat-out run for yardage. Wilson suddenly was targeted more, which means his catches increased. In five games, Wilson had double-digit targets, including a season-high 18 in Week 10 against the San Francisco 49ers. He ended the season with 126 targets, 78 receptions for 1,006 yards, and seven tuddies. Quite a bit of a difference from starting the season with 18 targets, 8 receptions for 52 yards, and one score. But some have mentioned that Wilson played great while Harrison was out and had minimal stats when Harrison and other receivers returned to the lineup. Cardinals Insider Kyle Odegard mentioned this regarding the franchise giving an extension now to Wilson instead of waiting to see if he could have some consistency in multiple seasons: “This is a tricky negotiation to me. Put up crazy numbers when MHJ was hurt and very little when everyone was healthy. Cardinals should try to slow-play it, while Wilson needs to play hardball and try to get a deal done.” And now, Wilson has an up-to-date deal. What are folks saying about the new contract? Bryan DeArdo – CBS Sports “Wilson has parlayed his breakout 2025 season into a life-altering contract extension. Making Wilson’s success even more impressive is the fact that he was often the primary focus of opposing defenses. There was a good chance it would rise again if he was able to duplicate or exceed last year’s numbers this season. Instead of paying more or potentially losing him in free agency, the Cardinals chose to take care of Wilson now while keeping him under contract for the foreseeable future.” Josh Weinfuss – ESPN Arizona “Wilson’s final average per year is almost $10 million more than what was initially offered, a source said. The deal took months because whenever Wilson’s team countered, the Cardinals would raise their offer incrementally, the source added, causing negotiations to become stale in training camp. It was Wilson who decided on a three-year contract instead of four years, according to the source.” Jeremy Bergman – NFL.com “Wilson logged his first 1,000-yard season in 2025, hauling in seven touchdowns on 78 receptions and targeted by Cardinals quarterbacks a career-high 126 times. As the campaign wore on and Arizona fell out of playoff contention, Wilson saw even more action. His target share rose from 11.0% over the first five weeks to 23.2% from Week 6 on, per NFL Pro, as Arizona was trailing or tied on 651 of 769 plays (84.7%) from Week 6 through the regular season, the fifth-highest rate in the NFL. With a young roster and first-year head coach in Mike LaFleur, the Cardinals will at least have the steady Wilson to look to, for now and the years to come.” "From the bottom of my heart I want to say thank you to the entire organization and fanbase for having so much support for me" – @mikewilllyy ❤️ pic.twitter.com/zr2SP8wfMB — Arizona Cardinals (@AZCardinals) September 3, 2026 Darren Urban – azcardinals.com “On Thursday, Wilson and the team made sure that viewpoint would not change anytime soon. He had been scheduled to become a free agent at season’s end, but signed a three-year contract extension. Mike LaFleur found Wilson right before the signing to give him a congratulatory hug and left clapping enthusiastically for the move. He had been a steady pass catcher through most of his career, but after Jacoby Brissett took over as quarterback in the sixth game of 2025, Wilson’s play and production hit a new level. He wanted to be in Arizona. And he’s glad it turned out that way.” Tyler Drake – Arizona Sports “Wilson emerged as a true WR1 for the franchise with injuries and inconsistency plaguing Marvin Harrison Jr.; Wilson stepped into a much larger role midway through the year. Throughout training camp and the preseason, the wide receiver has flashed all the intangibles needed to take over the Puka Nacua role in head coach Mike LaFleur’s offense. Whether he’s playing the Z, X, Y, or running the rock, Wilson looks poised to produce in Arizona’s new-look offense.” Rob Maaddi – Yahoo! Sports “Wilson became the latest NFL wide receiver to land a lucrative deal before the season. Wilson is coming off his best NFL season in 2025. The extension is worth $75 million, including $47 million guaranteed, and has a maximum value of $78 million. He’s the latest in a growing list of top receivers to get paid handsomely since March.” Adam La Rose – Pro Football Rumors “Wilson has seen his…

full_text: PISCATAWAY, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 29: KJ Duff #8 of the Rutgers Scarlet Knights catches a pass against Audavion Collins #2 of the Penn State Nittany Lions in the fourth quarter at SHI Stadium on November 29, 2025 in Piscataway, New Jersey. The Penn State Nittany Lions defeated the Rutgers Scarlet Knights 40-36. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images If Week 0 was the appetizer and Saturday, September 5th is the entree, then Thursday, September 3rd is the unlimited bread that is served at the table. College football is back, and it’s looking to be an exciting season full of storylines galore. But if you’re an Atlanta Falcons fan, you’re looking for more. You’re looking for a potential new quarterback, an offensive tackle to finally let Jake Matthews rest or upgrade after Kaleb McGary’s retirement, a safety to usurp the Jessie Bates role when he retires or his play falls off, another defensive tackle in case the trades involving Gervon Dexter Sr. or Maason Smith don’t work out, etc. There are plenty of avenues this Falcons team can take, but for now, here are five 2027 NFL Draft prospects to watch this Thursday as college football season returns. KJ Duff, WR, Rutgers vs. UMass, 6 pm, Big Ten Network Height: 6’6” Weight: 219 KJ Duff 5 REC, 127 YDS, 1 TD vs Penn State Today. 6'6 absolute freak. pic.twitter.com/w1uuOjf661 https://t.co/SA1CIqBvC0 — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 30, 2025 By the end of this cycle, Duff will probably have played his way into the back half of the first round, but if he’s there at the top of the 2nd (or the back half of the 1st, depending on how this season goes), Duff would be a great addition to the receiver room beside Drake London and Zachariah Branch. Duff has unbelievable size that amounts to an enormous catch radius. Add in his movement skills being akin to someone about three inches shorter, and you have a dangerous weapon on the outside. A dangerous enough weapon that you fully unlock London’s potential as a power slot. Davaughn Patterson, Safety, Wake Forest vs. Akron, 7 pm, ACC Network Height: 6’1” Weight: 215 Some defenders fill a position. Davaughn Patterson fills whatever position Wake Forest needs. @sethdowdle explains why he could be the Demon Deacons’ ultimate defensive problem solver in 2026. ⬇️ https://t.co/LKwRdjLHJJ pic.twitter.com/eaE6EDYtv4 — Barry Lewis (@BarryRLewis) August 4, 2026 With offenses becoming bigger, the defenses have to keep up and get bigger themselves. You see these big nickel players: Nick Emmanwori, Kyle Hamilton, even Cooper DeJean, bigger defensive backs that can play the run like a safety and cover tight ends and slot receivers like a cornerback. Safety Davaughn Patterson is one of those players. At 6’1”, 215, Patterson is a safety who has shown the ability to do just that. He is one of the more important players on the Deamon Deacons defense and you will see him all over the field for them this season. title: Ian Cunningham: Falcons still deciding QB battle
summary: Who is going to start for the Atlanta Falcons at the quarterback position against the Pittsburgh Steelers? We still don’t know, and with the Raiders making Kirk Cousins their official Week 1 starter, the Falcons are the last team still without a named Week 1 starter. We will know soon, though. In remarks to the […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 14: Tua Tagovailoa #1 of the Atlanta Falcons warms up alongside Michael Penix Jr. #9 prior to an NFL preseason game against the Denver Broncos at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Who is going to start for the Atlanta Falcons at the quarterback position against the Pittsburgh Steelers? We still don’t know, and with the Raiders making Kirk Cousins their official Week 1 starter, the Falcons are the last team still without a named Week 1 starter. We will know soon, though. In remarks to the media on Wednesday, Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham said the Falcons want to see more from all four quarterbacks, but particularly Michael Penix Jr. as he is finally cleared and able to practice fully. The Falcons and Penix decided he wasn’t ready to go for the preseason finale, but the hope is that he can show he’s ready to go for the regular season. Cunningham said the #Falcons want to see more from the QBs, specifically seeing Penix in more full practices, before making a decision. — Marc Raimondi (@marcraimondi) September 2, 2026 Penix is competing with Tua Tagovailoa, with Cooper Rush and Jack Strand there as veteran insurance and a developmental option, respectively. The best outcome for the Falcons is Penix taking the job and never looking back, playing well enough to cement himself as the long-term starter for this team and helping to lift this Falcons offense to new heights. Is it the most realistic outcome, though? I’m not so sure. I continue to believe that Tua will be your Week 1 starter, and reporting from NFL insider Cameron Wolfe suggests that Tua “helped himself” over the past two weeks, that Penix will start eventually, and the team’s need to name a Week 1 starter will not translate to the team rushing Penix to be ready if he’s not. The picture painted by that report, by Penix’s timeline to this point, and the fact that he wasn’t able to get into the final preseason game suggest heavily that Penix would need to make significant strides and impress to be out there against Pittsburgh. That’s hardly an impossibility—Penix has real talent and has done a great job rehabbing to this point—but the breadth of everything we’ve seen and heard this summer suggests it’s still less likely than a healthy Tua simply beginning the year as a starter. Falcons new regime: president of 🏈 Matt Ryan, HC Kevin Stefanski & GM Ian Cunningham will be collaborative in QB1 decision. But it’s prove it time for Penix & Tua with 2027 draft decision in deeper QB class looming: pic.twitter.com/h6GUzyuyXr — Cameron Wolfe (@CameronWolfe) September 3, 2026 I would draw your attention to Wolfe’s “eventually” here, though. I firmly believe Tua has to be lights out to hold Penix off for any longer than the first month of the season, both because Tua is here for a single season and because Penix offers upside Tua simply doesn’t. Penix also has a fifth-year option that the Falcons need to pick up in April, as the AJC’s Daniel Flick wrote , and it would be very helpful for the new regime to get an extended look at him to figure out if they’re going to pick that option up. Cunningham also explained why the Falcons kept four quarterbacks, as AtlantaFalcons.com reporter Will McFadden relayed : “To see Coop and Jack continuously to get better throughout, while Tua and Mike were getting healthy. Coming in with that, thinking, alright, there’s some injury risk with those guys, trying to protect against that,” Cunningham said. “There’s a little bit of an insurance policy, but there’s also these guys who have been productive during the preseason. “And so, if you let a guy like Cooper go, there’s a potential that he may be able to get an opportunity to go to another team. If you let a guy like Jack Strand go, he’s subject to waivers. And the way he played. We talk about all the time draft, develop, retain—in his case, he was undrafted, but to develop. There’s a chance that somebody could have claimed him. I think it’s about living in the now but also living in the future with Jack. So that kind of went into the four-quarterback thought process.” The long and short of it is that for at least the early portion of the season, it seems likely the Falcons will carry four quarterbacks, and that Tua will be in the driver’s seat Week 1 barring a terrific couple of weeks of practice from Penix Penix overtaking him this week, chances are the Falcons will announce their starter by the middle of next week at the latest. I’m still hopeful it will be Penix against Pittsburgh, but I’m not holding my breath.

title: Ravens announce season-long captains and leadership team
summary: In a break from previous tradition, the Baltimore Ravens will have season-long player captains this coming season. Previously under John Harbaugh, the Ravens would rotate different captains each week, but new head coach Jesse Minter is opting for a new approach. The captains were decided via a vote from the players this week and the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 09: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens gives a play call to Derrick Henry #22 against the Minnesota Vikings in the first quarter of a 2025 NFL game at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 09, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images In a break from previous tradition, the Baltimore Ravens will have season-long player captains this coming season. Previously under John Harbaugh, the Ravens would rotate different captains each week, but new head coach Jesse Minter is opting for a new approach. The captains were decided via a vote from the players this week and the results were as follows: QB Lamar Jackson RB Derrick Henry DL Calais Campbell LB Roquan Smith S Kyle Hamilton Our 2026 captains and leadership team‼️ pic.twitter.com/ABwCLJsT5a — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) September 3, 2026 The Ravens will also have a leadership team that features five other veterans, in addition to the team captains: TE Mark Andrews, WR Zay Flowers, LS Nick Moore, OT Ronnie Stanley and EDGE Trey Hendrickson. Many other teams around the league similarly have season-long captains, but this is a first for the Ravens and another change to user in a new era. The captain selections are not surprising, although it is noteworthy that Campbell was voted despite having just signed with the team again. That speaks to the respect he garners from teammates and his first-class leadership skills on and off the field. Jackson and Henry are obvious choices on offense, as are Hamilton and Smith on defense. Smith has been the leading communicator and energizer of the Ravens’ defense since arriving a few years ago, and Hamilton has grown into a leadership role in short order as a four-year veteran. In years past, the Ravens had a small “leadership council” of players during Harbaugh’s tenure, featuring the likes of Jackson, Stanley, Marlon Humphrey, and Matthew Judon, among others. This new leadership team is likely a similar concept but expands the group of players a bit. A somewhat surprising exclusion from both the captains and leadership team is Humphrey, who is the second-most tenured player on the roster behind Stanley.

summary: The Baltimore Ravens re-signed undrafted rookie cornerback Lardarius Webb Jr. – son of longtime Ravens defensive back Lardarius Webb – to their practice squad on Thursday, per a team announcement. Webb, 23, originally signed with the Ravens this spring as an undrafted rookie out of Wake Forest. He was one of several young cornerbacks to […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Lardarius Webb Jr. #34 of the Baltimore Ravens stands for the National Anthem before an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens re-signed undrafted rookie cornerback Lardarius Webb Jr. – son of longtime Ravens defensive back Lardarius Webb – to their practice squad on Thursday, per a team announcement. Webb, 23, originally signed with the Ravens this spring as an undrafted rookie out of Wake Forest. He was one of several young cornerbacks to flash in training camp, with one particularly memorable pass breakup in the end zone that brought the rest of the defense onto the field in celebration. Webb played in all three preseason games with time at outside and slot cornerback. His 5-foot-9, 168-pound frame struggled to hold up against the run, but he looked confident and comfortable in coverage. He flashed on special teams during last Friday’s win over the Commanders, making two tackles and forcing a fumble. Though that was not enough to make the initial 53-man roster, he will still have a chance to contribute this year from the practice squad. The Ravens released veteran cornerback Amani Oruwariye from their practice squad to make room for Webb’s return. The 30-year-old offers solid depth on special teams – he did so in Baltimore last year – but Webb is a younger player with more appealing developmental curve. The Ravens also formalized the signing of veteran offensive lineman Chuma Edoga to their practice squad on Thursday. Undrafted rookie center Nick Dawkins was released in a corresponding move, leaving the team without a third center. Starting right guard Vega Ioane said after practice ( via The Athletic’s Jeff Zrebiec ) that he took snaps at center in case of emergency. The first-round pick snapping the ball in the regular season would certainly be a five-alarm fire in Baltimore, so Dawkins could find his way back to the practice squad in the near future.

title: Ar’maj Reed provides Buffalo Bills with immense upside at guard in long-term future
summary: I owe it to myself to write about Bills rookie guard Ar’maj Reed-Adams, but not as a victory lap. Quite simply, Reed-Adams was one of my 2026 draft crushes, so I would’ve been “rooting” for him regardless of NFL locale. He wasn’t selected until the seventh round by the Bills, and then actually made Buffalo’s […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 27: Ar'maj Reed-Adams #60 of the Buffalo Bills looks to make a block during a pre-season game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Highmark Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images I owe it to myself to write about Bills rookie guard Ar’maj Reed-Adams, but not as a victory lap. Quite simply, Reed-Adams was one of my 2026 draft crushes, so I would’ve been “rooting” for him regardless of NFL locale. He wasn’t selected until the seventh round by the Bills, and then actually made Buffalo’s 53-man roster after the preseason. Based on his draft position alone — heck, he was one of the last 20 picks in the draft — Reed-Adams was a relative long-shot for such an achievement. In fact, 18 of the 41 seventh-round picks from the 2026 NFL Draft were waived by cutdown day, and as you can probably imagine, the seventh round historically has the highest rate of players who are waived after their first training camp and preseason with the team that drafted them. I had a third-round grade on Reed-Adams before the draft. He was my IOL5. Here’s my pre-draft scouting report on him : “ Ar’maj Reed-Adams is a tall, long, well-built guard with a rare, almost unmatched wingspan and a frame that can still comfortably add more mass. He carries his weight well for his height and plays with good hip roll out of his stance. His length is a true weapon — he consistently deploys it to keep defenders off his frame and stay attached through reps. While not an immediate, effortless anchor, he shows the ability to sink his pads and grow roots as the play develops, and his balance recovery is strong even when initially stressed. In the run game, Reed-Adams brings above-average movement skills for his size and enough range to execute down blocks, combo climbs, and reach assignments. He’s not a super explosive or ultra-fluid space mover, but he’s far from limited and can get his hands on defenders consistently. He flashes a developing mean streak and uses his length to control reps, though he does have a tendency to lean into blocks at times, which can open him up to counters. At the second level, he can be a half-step late or slightly off-balance initially, but typically recalibrates and finishes the rep. In pass protection, his length, awareness, and ability to absorb counters stand out. He does an excellent job staying attached to interior defenders and using his reach to mirror and control rushers even when initially challenged. His hands are active and reasonably heavy, with solid grip strength that plays up because of his length. He’s a plus stunt and blitz recognizer and rarely looks out of position. Overall, this is a highly experienced, pro-ready guard with rare length and strong technical foundations who needs to add 5–10% more functional strength to unlock a high-end ceiling .” I viewed him as a ready-to-go blocker. Really did. And I was enamored with his physical measurements, especially in a league that is prioritizing size and length at every position along the offensive line. Per MockDraftable , Adams’ 34 3/8” arm length places in the 88th percentile at the guard position. He’s 6’6”, which places in the 91st percentile. And his weight of 314 pounds was only in the 54th percentile, meaning he has plenty of room to grow into his towering frame. Offensive linemen getting bigger and stronger might be the easiest part of being in the NFL. With Bills new offensive line coach Pat Meyer being a disciple of Aaron Kromer, you can bet your bottom dollar Buffalo will continue to prioritize size and power up front. By next season, Reed-Adams can very easily take the field as a 325-330 pound guard, standing 6’6” with elite length. And his showing in his first preseason was dazzling. I zeroed in on him often. On 103 pass-blocking snaps… zero pressures allowed. Only one holding penalty. No false starts. While he’s only a rookie, Reed-Adams played over 2,300 snaps across six seasons at Kansas and A&M and will turn 25 in November. I typically gravitate toward younger players in the draft, but along the offensive line, I’m OK with older prospects if they enter the league with ample experience (and, of course, were dominant players at the collegiate level). Reed-Adams surrendered just two sacks on his 739 pass-blocking snaps with the Aggies in 2024 and 2025 combined. He was a team captain in 2025. Of course, the Bills extended right guard O’Cyrus Torrence in August, and that’s the position Reed-Adams played at Texas A&M. Yet he took 78 preseason snaps at left guard and didn’t look out of place whatsoever. While I’m here on Torrence, quite frankly, I think there are a lot of similarities between the two — size, length, strengths, and weaknesses. Alec Anderson won the starting left guard over veteran Austin Corbett for this season. Both Anderson and Corbett are playing on one-year deals with the Bills in 2026. Reed-Adams is waiting in the wings as a serious starting left guard candidate for 2027. And his quietly impressive summer will probably factor into any future contract talks with Anderson and/or Corbett if either play particularly well this season. And, at the risk of going overboard here, I believe the Bills could do much worse than Reed-Adams if he was forced onto the field in a regular-season game as a rookie. If Reed-Adams becomes a quality guard in Orchard Park, he’d join the increasingly long list of Day 3 gems uncovered by Brandon Beane and his scouting staff. And, heck, because I thought Reed-Adams should’ve been a Day 2 pick, I probably feel more confident than any analyst he will indeed mature into a sturdy blocker for the Bills.

ConnectLife has three donation centers; with locations in Tonawanda, West Seneca, and Williamsville. But that’s not all! title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 9 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 29: Jake Delhomme #17 of the Carolina Panthers passes against the New York Jets at Giants Stadium on November 29, 2009 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Nick Laham/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #9. Jake Delhomme We’re inside the top 10 now, which means we’ve got fan favorites all over the place. Today, we look at one of the most widely liked fan favorites of all time, the Ragin’ Cajun himself, Jake Delhomme. Delhomme had one of the more unlikely rises to starting NFL quarterback that you’ll ever see, though in hindsight, there were some early signs of future success. He played college football at what was then known as Southwestern Louisiana (now known as University of Louisiana at Lafeyette). There, starting in his freshman year, he was a standout passer at the mid-major level. Despite a decorated career and some elite counting stats, Delhomme went undrafted and signed up the road with the New Orleans Saints. He spent a couple of years on the Saints practice squad and in NFL Europe, where he backed up Kurt Warner one year and won a championship the next as part of a two quarterback system. He ended up spending six seasons in New Orleans but rarely saw the field, though he did show some promise in some fill-in duty and in the preseason. He finally escaped New Orleans in search of a starting gig and found his way to Carolina, who had just gone 7-9 with 36 year old journeyman Rodney Peete as their starter. He started the opener on the bench, but it didn’t take long for his number to get called. After a first half that saw the Panthers pick up one first down while gaining a total of 16 yards (after losing a total of 18 yards over their last three drives), John Fox went with Delhomme. The Panthers wouldn’t look back. Delhomme would lead four scoring drives (while also throwing two interceptions), the last of which ended with the game winning touchdown to Ricky Proehl with 16 seconds left. That half a game would prove to be the perfect encapsulation of the Jake Delhomme experience. He ended up leading the Cardiac Cats to a surprise appearance in the Super Bowl with five fourth quarter comebacks and seven game winning drives in the fourth quarter during the regular season and one more game winning drive in the playoffs. He went toe to toe with Tom Brady in the Super Bowl and threw what still stands as the longest pass in Super Bowl history, but he and the Panthers came up short in the game. He was never the most efficient passer, and he was prone to turning the ball over with his gunslinging ways, but he gave his guys a chance and he wasn’t afraid to force the issue. And he always saved his best play for when the stakes were the highest. He earned a Pro Bowl nomination in 2005 and led the Panthers to an 11-5 record. His performance took a slight dip in 2006, and that would prove to be early signs of the approaching fall off. He started the 2007 season very strong but suffered an elbow injury in Week 3 that would ultimately require Tommy John surgery. He would return to throw a game winning touchdown on the final play of Week 1 of the 2008 season. He would recapture his Cardiac Cat magic with another four fourth quarter comebacks and five game winning drive, but he finished the season with just 15 touchdowns against 12 interceptions. The season ended with one of if not the most depressing performances Panthers fans have seen. He threw five interceptions and lost a fumble in a 33-14 beatdown at the hands of the Cardinals, and he would never be the same. Fresh off a new contract extension, he turned the ball over five times in the season opener of the next season. Through six games, he had thrown just four touchdowns while getting picked off 13 times and losing a pair of fumbles. He would finish that season with eight touchdowns and 21 turnovers. That would be the end of his career in Carolina. He went on to spend a mess of a season in Cleveland in 2010. Then, in 2011, he was brought in by the Texans as an emergency backup with a couple of their quarterbacks on the shelf. He came off the bench in the last game of the season and almost ended his career just the way it started, with a game winning drive with just 14 seconds on the clock. Unfortunately, a botched snap ruined the potential game winning 2-point conversion, and that would be the last snap of Delhomme’s career. Delhomme is about as pure a Carolina Panther as there is. He remained a very vocal fan of the team after his retirement and rejoined the organization as a color commentator on the radio broadcast, where he still refers to the Panthers with “we” and “our” pronouns when calling the game. Few players are as synonymous with the Panthers as Delhomme, and for that, he lands at number nine in the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 10 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE , NC - NOVEMBER 16: Dan Morgan #55 of the Carolina Panthers participates in warm-ups before a game against the Washington Redskins on November 16, 2003 at Ericsson Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Sporting News via Getty Images via Getty Images) | Sporting News via Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #10. Dan Morgan There aren’t many people in NFL history who had successful careers on the field and turned that into notable, successful careers in NFL front offices, especially for the team they played for. Dan Morgan is already in rarified air from an NFL history perspective, but his skill on the field and as GM (so far) have both been above average. Morgan ended his collegiate career at The U with a dominant senior year. The awards flooded in for that 2000 season: Big East Defensive Player of the Year, Bronko Nagurski Award, Chuck Bednarik Award, Dick Butkus Award, and unanimous First Team All-American. The following 2001 NFL Draft, the Panthers used the 11th overall pick to take Morgan, immediately bolstering their defense. Despite his ability on the field, his body could not handle the NFL game on a regular basis. Morgan started 11 games at strong side linebacker his rookie year, making the All-Rookie Team. That season could have been even more exceptional, but Morgan broke his leg late in the season and was put on IR. He returned the following year and took over the middle of the defense. Groin and shoulder injuries limited Morgan to just eight games his sophomore season, but he was dynamic in the games he played. He was able to recover a bit in the 2003 season as he helped captain the dominant Panthers defense on their first Super Bowl run in franchise history. A pulled hammy and his first career concussion limited him to just 11 regular season games, but he was healthy and dominant in the postseason, including a still Super Bowl record 18 tackles against the Patriots. His health stayed solid in 2004 as well, allowing him to play in 12 games and earn his first and only Pro Bowl selection. He tallied 102 tackles, two sacks, two interceptions, a forced fumble, two fumble recoveries, and six passes defended. In 2005, he played a career-high 13 games and was a force on the field, though his counting stats took a dip. Unfortunately, the 2006 season was the beginning of the end physically for Dan Morgan. He missed the final 15 games after suffering two severe concussions within a month. He came back for the 2007 season with specialized padding and a protective mouthpiece, which seemed to be working. Concussions weren’t the death knell, though, it was an Achilles tear in Week 3 that did him in. He tried to make a comeback with the New Orleans Saints in both 2008 and 2009, but his physical health denied him the opportunity to see the field. He immediately transitioned to the front office side of the NFL, joining the Seahawks as a scouting intern in 2010. He was promoted to Assistant Director of Pro Personnel in 2011, then became the Seahawks Director of Pro Personnel in 2015 after helping the team win the Super Bowl. In 2018, Morgan moved to the Buffalo Bills and was given the Director of Player Personnel position directly under General Manager (and former Panthers front office member) Brandon Beane. Morgan returned to Carolina in 2021 as the Assistant General Manager under Scott Fitterer. After Fitterer was relieved of his duties in 2024, Morgan took the interim job and made enough of an impression that he was hired as the full time replacement. He has been the Panthers General Manager since then, playing a major role in the upward trajectory the last couple of seasons including hiring Dave Canales, drafting some young and promising players, filling major holes in free agency, and making shrewd trades for veteran contributors. While he has definitely taken his lumps and learned on the fly, he seems to be steering the ship in the right direction. While his playing career was shortened by injuries, his dominance while on the field and his decisions so far as GM land him in the top ten on our list.

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: What defines a successful 2026?
summary: Ask this question in any of the last 6+ years, and you would get something to the tune of: “A successful Bears season looks like QB development, improvement by (rattles off a handful of key players) and threaten for a playoff spot” But 2025 changed that. The Bears won their division, won a playoff game, […]
full_text: Dec 20, 2025; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) runs onto the field during player introductions before the game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: David Banks-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Ask this question in any of the last 6+ years, and you would get something to the tune of: “A successful Bears season looks like QB development, improvement by (rattles off a handful of key players) and threaten for a playoff spot” But 2025 changed that. The Bears won their division, won a playoff game, and unearthed a QB+Coach combo that we have been clamoring for for years. So with the 2026 season a week away, expectations have changed. We can no longer just ask for development and to threaten for a playoff spot. What defines a successful 2026 Bears campaign? I won’t be satisfied unless they make the NFC Championship Game. They need to make real progress in the playoffs after last season. This is no easy task, though. Every team in the league is looking to take the “next step”, and unfortunately there aren’t enough spots in the dance to accommodate them all. In fact, the Bears haven’t made consecutive playoff appearances since the 2005 and 2006 seasons, where they showed true incremental progress in improving on a Divisional Round appearance to a Super Bowl appearance. Before that, the Bears haven’t shown sustained playoff success since the stretch of 1984 to 1991, where they made the playoffs in 7 of 8 seasons, winning a Super Bowl and making the Conference Championship in two other seasons. So linear improvement is not guaranteed. Beyond a NFCCG appearance, I think a few other things would help me define this as a successful season. Caleb Williams cements himself as an elite QB by introducing consistency to his moments of genius. Ben Johnson proves he is one of the few HCs that can churn out perennial winning football teams. The Bears pass-catchers all take steps forward, with one of Odunze/Burden/Loveland emerging as a top-tier player at their position. One young defensive player catapults themself into a “feature role”. This could be Jordan van den Berg, Austin Booker, Dillon Thieneman, or a number of other guys. Dennis Allen shows he is the right complement to Ben Johnson by developing and scheming the talent into more consistent performances. It’s unlikely that all of the above hit, but I also don’t think it is far-fetched to think that they can. Bears fans this offseason have been excited, but as we approach the season and some realities creep in (injuries, trades, etc) you can feel expectations tempering. Part of this is the conditioning we have gone through as Bears fans — to never expect too much of our team. But I think it’s time to change that narrative. Expect a lot out of this group. This team is different. Now it’s your turn! What defines a successful 2026 Bears season to you? Sound off in the comments!

title: NFL Week 1 Power Rankings and the Biggest Question for Each Team
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season is upon us, and it’s felt like forever since a meaningful football game was played. With training camp and the preseason in the rearview mirror, the time for football to take over our lives is here. Before another exciting season kicks off, we decided to take a deeper dive into […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - JANUARY 14: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on from the sideline prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on January 14, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Ryan Kang/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season is upon us, and it’s felt like forever since a meaningful football game was played. With training camp and the preseason in the rearview mirror, the time for football to take over our lives is here. Before another exciting season kicks off, we decided to take a deeper dive into the offseason that was and how each team ranks heading into Week 1. Without further ado, let’s take a look at our WCG pre-Week 1 Power Rankings. 1. Seattle Seahawks 2026 Question To Answer: Are the Seahawks the most overlooked Super Bowl winner in recent memory? Heading into the season, it feels like there’s much more focus on other teams than the group that completely dominated their way through the playoffs and into a Super Bowl victory. Perception is in the eye of the beholder, and it’s worth noting that no one had the Seahawks as a Super Bowl contender this time last year. That said, this is an extremely well-rounded roster that might not have the same flashy offseason as a team like the Rams or Chiefs, but might still have the best overall roster in the league. 2. Los Angeles Rams 2026 Question To Answer: Will going all-in once again pay off for the Rams in what could be one of Matthew Stafford’s final seasons? Only time will tell how many more years Stafford will play, but it’s clear that general manager Les Snead and company see a win-now window and have no issue saying “f them picks” yet again. The trade for Myles Garrett shocked the NFL world. Couple that with the return of Aaron Donald, even on a rotational basis, and they’ve got all the pieces to have a dominant Super Bowl-winning season. Now all that is left to do is deliver on expectations. 3. Denver Broncos 2026 Question To Answer: Can a healthy Bo Nix be enough to get them to the Super Bowl in 2026? I’m still not sure the Broncos would have won the Super Bowl even if Nix wasn’t hurt, but it’s hard to imagine they wouldn’t have put up a better fight than the Patriots did. The AFC West, assuming the Chiefs round back into form, will be tougher in 2026. Even so, the Broncos are a well-built team with a true No. 1 receiver and one of the league’s elite defenses. Even if Nix fails to take another step in his development, this group should be good enough to challenge for a title. I don’t think they have enough to win it. 4. Buffalo Bills 2026 Question To Answer: How will (or won’t) the decision to replace Sean McDermott with Sean Brady pay off? 2025 felt like the best opportunity for the Bills to break through and win the AFC. Following a disappointing exit during the Divisional Round, Buffalo decided it was time to make a change. While it’s hard to blame them in some ways, they took a serious gamble in letting go of McDermott for a first-time candidate in Brady. This roster has some flaws, but a change in leadership/messaging and a player like DJ Moore should be enough to get them over the hump. 5. New England Patriots 2026 Question To Answer: Can the Patriots overcome an offseason full of distractions, or will they prove to be the beneficiaries of last year’s easy schedule? On paper, New England is a very talented team. That said, there’s a strong argument to be made that they were the beneficiaries of one of the league’s easiest schedules and a team that, in general, played over their heads. While I’d give the Bills better odds to win the division, if the Patriots can ignore the distractions caused by their head coach, there are plenty of reasons to believe they could be even better in 2026. Much of that comes down to Drake Maye refining his game and A.J. Brown delivering one of his best years. 6. San Francisco 49ers 2026 Question To Answer: Are the 49ers for real, or will last year’s surprise season prove to be an overachievement? Heading into last season, many believed the 49ers were simply playing out the string of a retool that would require a tough season of taking on oodles of dead cap space to get back into contention. Instead of a fourth-place finish like many projected, they rounded back into playoff form and came close to winning the division. This is a talented, but older roster that is in a much better financial state moving forward. Will that be enough to win the division or have post-season success? We’ll see. 7. Baltimore Ravens 2026 Question To Answer: Will replacing John Harbaugh prove to be the needed move to get the Ravens back to a serious Super Bowl contender? Like the Bills, the Ravens felt a change was needed after their Harbaugh-led squad failed to make the playoffs, thanks to a down season and a missed field goal with time expiring in Week 18. There’s no question about Harbaugh’s ability as a coach, but sometimes fresh ideas are what are needed to get a team back over the top. This is a young coaching staff with plenty of talent, but unlocking Lamar Jackson will be key to any Super Bowl aspirations. 8. Houston Texans 2026 Question To Answer: Can C.J. Stroud prove to be an above-average quarterback, or will his historical rookie performance prove to be the outlier? There’s no questioning the Texans’ defense. They are about as elite as elite comes. The issue is that in the AFC, they need an offense that can outplay some of the conference’s other elite defenses. Much of that starts with quarterback play, where, frankly, Stroud has failed to live up to expectations after an impressive rookie campaign. Last year’s playoff performance was one of the worst we’ve seen in quite a while. Although they continue to praise Stroud publicly, this feels like a big year for the fourth-year quarterback to prove he’s worthy of a high-dollar extension and capable of being good enough in a stacked conference of top-end quarterbacks. 9. Chicago Bears 2026 Question To Answer: Can Caleb Williams take the next step into quarterback stardom? Year 1 of the Williams and Ben Johnson marriage didn’t get off to the best of starts, but by the time their season ended, the Bears’ offense showed plenty of promise. No one has ever doubted Williams’ big-play ability or athleticism, but the next step in his development is making the easy plays look… Well, easy. If he can do that, it’s easy to envision a scenario where he climbs into the Top 5-7 range. Step 1 will be getting his completion percentage up, which was the worst of any qualifying starting quarterback in the league last season. 10. Kansas City Chiefs 2026 Question To Answer: Will 2025 prove to be an “off year” or is the Chiefs’ window actually closing? Last season could not have gone much worse for the Chiefs, no matter how you slice it. Missing the playoffs is one thing, but losing your star quarterback that late into the season with a serious knee injury is even more challenging. On the plus side, Patrick Mahomes will be ready for Week 1, and it appears that it took a losing season for them to upgrade the soft spots of their roster. This group is one year removed from back-to-back Super Bowl appearances. Now they must prove last year was a fluke, not the end of a dominant era. 11. Detroit Lions 2026 Question To Answer: Did Dan Campbell successfully replace Ben Johnson, or will another botched hire cost the Lions another year of their window? Detroit’s overall offensive numbers still ranked Top 10 in the league, but that was more talent-based than anything to do with coaching. Campbell did a solid job taking over playcalling duties, but he’s at his best as a head coach when he’s playing the CEO role. While many will think of Johnson as a great hire, his track record since being promoted to OC leaves plenty to be desired. This feels like a scenario where another failed hire could lead to a piping hot seat by year’s end. 12. Philadelphia Eagles 2026 Question To…

title: Is Kentavius Street really the best Chicago Bears defensive tackle?
summary: After the trade of Gervon Dexter, most of us Chicago Bears fans just assumed that Neville Gallimore and Grady Jarrett would be the starting defensive tackles on the team. Jarrett got a decent chunk of change from the Bears last year, and Gallimore was given a healthy raise when they brought him in as a […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 23 : Kentavius Street #93 of the Atlanta Falcons runs across the field during an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on November 23, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the trade of Gervon Dexter, most of us Chicago Bears fans just assumed that Neville Gallimore and Grady Jarrett would be the starting defensive tackles on the team. Jarrett got a decent chunk of change from the Bears last year, and Gallimore was given a healthy raise when they brought him in as a free agent in March. But Dennis Allen was addressing the media about his unit and said something that had some Bears fans buzzing. Dennis Allen said Kentavius Street had the best production of any DT in camp. Would have to think he's the favorite to start Week 1. — Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) September 2, 2026 Many Bears fans took this as a positive. The idea of Street being a surprise and elevating the unit. I don’t see it as a positive for Street; I see it as a negative for the rest of the defensive line. We know who Kentavius Street is already. There’s no reason to believe that he’s unlocked a new level of his talent. Street is a 30-year-old defensive tackle. He was a fourth-round selection by the San Francisco 49ers. He missed almost all of his first two seasons due to injury. He did play most of his final two seasons of his rookie contract with SF, but the 49ers didn’t see him as part of their future and they chose to let him go via free agency. He then went to the New Orleans Saints, signed a league minimum contract, and had a decent year as a rotational DT, but the Saints, like the Niners, chose to let him go via free agency. Street then got a contract from the Eagles in 2023. It was another league minimum deal. Later that year, Grady Jarrett (then of the Falcons) was injured, and Atlanta needed DL help and traded a 6th-round pick for Street. The Falcons decided to retain Street to a one year contract (his highest ever at $1.7 million per season), he had a pretty lackluster 2024 season, but they did bring him back in 2025 on a league minimum deal. However, Street didn’t make the 53-man roster, was cut during roster cutdowns, and spent most of the season on their practice squad. He was elevated late in the year and played pretty well the final few games of the season. But Street left Atlanta for another league minimum deal in Chicago. Why did I just spend paragraphs going through Street’s career? Because a tiger doesn’t change his stripes. Street is who he is. He’s been in the league for almost a decade and has been nothing more than a rotational defensive tackle. He has 10 career starts and spent most of last season on a practice squad. Defensive tackles who are 30 don’t suddenly become significant contributors. If Street is playing better than the rest of the team’s defensive tackles, that tells you the other tackles aren’t playing well, not that Street is. The Chicago Bears have a defensive tackle problem. This isn’t a new opinion; this is an opinion many have held all offseason. However, with that quote from Dennis Allen, the defensive line might be in even worse shape than even the most pessimistic of fans believed it was. Ben Johnson said everyone needs to coach better this year. Dennis Allen agreed with him. If Allen is going to unlock this defense, he may be the first person to make chicken salad out of chicken, you know what.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Which NFL GMs have had the most to work with in the Draft?
summary: From my own Bears-centric view of things, the Chicago Bears under Ryan Poles seem to have had a pretty rare set of conditions to help usher along a rebuild. In his first five years on the job, Poles had four selections in the top third of the first round (i.e. Top 11 picks) including the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - FEBRUARY 24: NFL Daily host Gregg Rosenthal interviews Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine on February 24, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images From my own Bears-centric view of things, the Chicago Bears under Ryan Poles seem to have had a pretty rare set of conditions to help usher along a rebuild. In his first five years on the job, Poles had four selections in the top third of the first round (i.e. Top 11 picks) including the #1 overall pick. He also made nine eight selections in the Top 50, and seventeen selections in the Top 100. How many GMs have enjoyed that much opportunity? Well, it depends. Obviously, the selections needed to be available under the same general manager. This excludes teams like Cleveland, which had back-to-back #1 selections in 2017 (Garrett) and 2018 (Mayfield) and seven top-ten picks in just nine years–but that was under six different managers . It also excludes Nick Cesario of Houston Texans, who would put up a good show but who only has three picks in the top eleven, even if all those were made within the top three . Likewise, if the sticking point is four elite selections, Trent Baalke doesn’t count either. He made back-to-back selections with the #1 overall pick (Lawrence and Walker), and despite having more pricey premium picks on a per-year basis than Poles (averaging 2,581 points on the Jimmy Johnson chart just in his four years, or the equivalent of having the #4 spot in the draft for four straight years), he didn’t qualify because his tenure was too short. Also not included, even though he would technically qualify, is Les Snead. He did in fact have four elite picks (and the #13 selection he used on Aaron Donald) in a 4-year stretch, but I intend on doing a larger piece later in the season looking at exactly how the Rams have defied convention on so many different fronts. For now, though, here are the other nine in ascending order of Top 11 draft picks made, with ties broken by average value of top picks made. Jason Licht (2014-present) Buccaneers Licht needed seven years to reach the playoffs, but when he got his team there, they won it all. His first six years averaged 2,358 points of premium draft selections per year and a .34 win rate, meaning he had more to work with but worse results than Poles has had to date. Of course, that championship the next year covers a lot. Key Selections : 4/18/31, meaning that he had 4 picks in the top eleven, 18 picks in the top fifty, and 31 in the first three rounds* with 19,457 in premium picks (1,621 per year) over his 12-year career. Record : 93-104 (.47 win) with a 6-4 record including a championship year Key Picks : Jameis Winston (#1), Devin White (#5), Mike Evans (#7), and Vernon Hargreaves III (#11) *All third-round tallies exclude those picks made in the compensatory pick range. Steve Keim (2013-2022) Cardinals Keim is a member of the “two quarterback club”, in that as a general manager he got two chances to draft his own passer. His decade in power in Arizona was ultimately pretty bland, with very middling results. Key Selection Ranges : 4/14/26 with 16,647 points in premium picks (1,665 per year) over his 10-year career Record : 80-80 in the regular season (.50 win), 1-3 in the playoffs Key Picks: Kyler Murray (#1), Jonathan Cooper (#7), Isaiah Simmons (#8), Josh Rosen (#10) Tom Telesco (2013-2023) Chargers The Chargers seem to have an identity as a team that feels like it should be doing more. Telesco had chances to build the team, but ultimately he couldn’t get them over the hump. Key Selection Ranges: 4/19/23 with 19,406 points in premium picks (1,764 per year) over his 11-year career. Record: 84-95 (.47 win) in the regular regular season, 2-3 in the playoffs Key Picks : Joey Bosa (#3), Justin Herbert (#6), Mike Willaims (#7), and DJ Fluker (#11) Mike Brown (2016-present) Bengals It’s difficult to know what to do with an owner-manager like Brown, so in the end I simply settled for taking a snapshot of the last ten years (2016-2025) for which we know the results, but it’s worth noting that the team would once again have picked in the top eleven in 2026 had they not traded #10 for Dexter Lawrence. Key Selection Ranges : 4/15/31 with 18,080 points in premium picks (1,808 per year) over the last ten years Record : 71-91-2 in the regular season (.44 win), but 5-2 in the playoffs Key Picks : Joe Burrow (#1), Ja’Marr Chase (#5), John Ross (#9), and Jonah Williams (#11) Terry Fontenot (2021-2025) Falcons Fontenot struggled over his five years, forcing ownership to bring in primary executive Matt Ryan to right the ship. He is one of only three on this list not to manage a playoff win, and he employed another. Key Selection Ranges: 4/10/17 with 11,361 points in premium picks (2,272 per year) over five years. Record: 37-48 (.32 win) in the regular season, no playoff appearances Key Picks: Kyle Pitts (#4), Drake London (#8), Bijan Robinson (#8), and Michael Penix (#8) Ryan Poles (2022-present) Bears Considered next to this group of his peers, Poles is in fact in the middle of his turnaround. Ten different general managers in the era of the CBA have had comparable draft choices available to them at the top, his actual rank among this group will probably be determined over the next few years. Key Selection Ranges : 4/9/17 with 11,034 points in premium picks (2,206 per year) spent over five years. This includes the #32 pick traded for Chase Claypool, which is probably unfair of me. It still feels “correct”, however. Record: 26-42 (.38 win) in the regular season, 1-1 in the playoffs Key Picks : Caleb Williams (#1), Rome Odunze (#9), Darnell Wright (#10), and Colston Loveland (#10). John Lynch (2017-present) 49ers Proof that having a number of premium picks is possible even for successful general managers, Lynch’s numbers benefit from Lance simply being considered the #2 overall pick and excluding trade information. Lynch has actually made more elite selections than Poles. However, four of those came within his first five years as GM. Key Selection Ranges : 5/13/24 with 16,755 in premium picks (1,676 per year) over his 10-year career. Record: 82-67 (.55 win) regular season record, 9-5 playoffs Key Picks: Trey Lance (#2), Nick Bosa (#3), Soloman Thomas (#3), Mike McGlinchey (#9), and Mykel Williams (#11). Ryan Pace (2015-2021) Bears Despite having a well-earned reputation for trading away picks, Pace made five selections in the top eleven, and never made a first-round pick out of this range. He is one of only three GMs on this list without a playoff win–and he worked for one of the others. Key Selection Ranges: 5/11/16 with 12,370 points in premium picks (1,767 per year) over his 7-year career. Record: 48-65 (.42 win) in the regular season, 0-2 in the playoffs Key Picks: Mitch Trubisky (#2), Kevin White (#7), Roquan Smith (#8), Leonard Floyd (#9), and Justin Fields (#11) Joe Douglas (2019-2024) Jets Douglas is only the third GM on this list without a playoff win, and he had the most to work with in terms of premium selection and year-to-year value. However, his team simply struggled despite accumulating a few star players. Key Selection Ranges: 5/11/16 with 14,707 premium picks (2,451 per year) over his 6-year career. Record: 32-68 (.32 win) in the regular season, no playoff appearances Key Picks : Zach Wilson (#2), Quinnen Williams (#3), Sauce Gardner (#4), Garrett Wilson (#10), and Mekhi Beckton (#11). David Caldwell (2013-2020) Jaguars Caldwell had more opportunity than any GM in this group by virtually every conceivable measure. More elite picks, more total value, and more year-to-year value. However, despite one playoff run, he actually has the worst record of all of these GMs (which explains the high selections, after all). However, the team clearly had little to show for all of that potential investment. Key Selection Ranges : 7/16/27 with 20,930 in premium picks…

title: Which Chicago Bears Practice Squad Player Will Make the Biggest Impact?
summary: With roster cuts in the rearview and practice squads across the league all but finalized for opening day, we ask the following question: Which current practice squad player will make the biggest impact? You can take a look at Chicago’s practice squad in depth here, but for me, this answer boils down to three players. […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 22: Chicago Bears wide receiver Kaden Davis (27) carries the ball during the preseason game between the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With roster cuts in the rearview and practice squads across the league all but finalized for opening day, we ask the following question: Which current practice squad player will make the biggest impact? You can take a look at Chicago’s practice squad in depth here , but for me, this answer boils down to three players. Salvon Ahmed – Running Back Ahmed was having a strong camp and explosive preseason before finally being cut and landing on the PS. Averaging 6 yards per carry and taking a screen pass 49 yards for a TD highlighted his training camp experience, but Ahmed routinely made plays in camp and looked every bit deserving of a roster spot. Kaden Davis – Wide Receiver Kaden Davis was my surprise of camp. Undrafted in the 2022 NFL Draft, Davis, AKA “White Lightning,” never recorded a single catch in the regular season and only returned four kickoffs – all with the Browns, according to Pro Football Reference. After spending time with the Lions practice squad, Davis showed up in Chicago and made more plays than arguably anyone else. I was actually expecting him to make the final 53, but not surprised to see him at least land on the PS. Marcus Davenport – DE Drafted in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft by the New Orleans Saints, Davenport joined Dennis Allen’s defense and notched 4.5 sacks as a rookie. Standing 6’6” and weighing 265lb (though I am guessing it’s much closer to 300 these days), Davenport is a prototypical Dennis Allen 4-3 DE. How much he has left in the tank, however, is another question. Especially after struggling through injuries his entire career and only once starting more than 9 games in a season. Added to a thin DE rotation, Davenport could be leaned upon heavily. My pick? Salvon Ahmed . The running back brought a burst that only starter D’Andre Swift possesses in both the run and pass game and comes in knowing new RB coach Eric Studesville’s run scheme, as he formerly played for Studesville in Miami. Weather it’s in the return game or spelling Swift and Monangai on offense, I expect Ahmed to have more of an impact than any other practice squad player in 2026. What about you? Which Practice Squad player do you feel makes the greatest impact this season?

title: Five as one: Bengals’ offensive line believes continuity can unlock full potential
summary: For most of the Joe Burrow era, the Cincinnati Bengals‘ offensive line has been something to worry about. Maybe it’s finally becoming something to believe in. And, if you listen to Amarius Mims and Dalton Risner, the reason goes well beyond blocking schemes, technique, or individual talent. It’s about five guys becoming one. Risner and […]
full_text: For most of the Joe Burrow era, the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ offensive line has been something to worry about. Maybe it’s finally becoming something to believe in. And, if you listen to Amarius Mims and Dalton Risner, the reason goes well beyond blocking schemes, technique, or individual talent. It’s about five guys becoming one. Risner and Mims sat down together recently for an exclusive interview with Bengals radio voice Dan Hoard , and what emerged was a picture of an offensive line that endured its share of struggles last season but came through them closer and better than when it started. “You see him growing, you see him want to be great,” Risner said of Mims. “He wants to be coached, he wants to see how he can get better. I love playing next to this guy. For years, Cincinnati has tried different combinations in front of Burrow, adding veterans through free agency and young players through the draft. This year, instead of rebuilding the offensive line yet again, the Bengals are bringing back all five starters: Orlando Brown Jr., Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras, Risner and Mims. And there are signs that continuity will pay off. The line struggled early last season but improved dramatically as the year progressed. Over the last seven games of the season, Pro Football Focus graded Cincinnati’s offensive line among the top five in the NFL. And PFF identified both Risner and Mims among the NFL’s most improved players at their respective positions over the second half of the season. Risner’s PFF grade improved from 56.8 over Weeks 1 through 9 to 79.6 from Weeks 10 through 18. Mims made an almost identical jump, going from 55.1 to 78.2. The improvement in Mims’ pass protection was particularly significant. After allowing 21 pressures and four sacks over the first nine weeks, the former first-round pick surrendered only 14 pressures and no sacks over the final eight. “The last seven or eight games is when it really started to gel,” Mims said. “We weren’t winning as much, but it was obvious we were getting better.” According to Mims, that improvement didn’t come because everything suddenly became easy. It came because the players learned how to deal with things going wrong. “It’s how you overcome those bad games,” Mims said. “I learned from guys like him [Risner] and Orlando: do not let one bad play affect the whole game. We’re in this together. O-line is hard. Five as one. It’s not going to be perfect. It’s just, how can we make this better?” That last phrase may be the key. Five as one. Offensive-line play depends on communication and trust more than any other position group on the field. One player can execute his assignment perfectly, and the play can still fail because of a missed protection or blown assignment somewhere else. Mims believes Cincinnati’s line learned to accept that reality and learned to trust one another. “We may not get the national credit,” Mims said. “As long as we know we have each other’s back, that’s all that matters.” Risner saw the same transformation. “We kept our heads on straight the whole year, kept working, kept working for each other,” he said. “We started to build this continuity. With time, we just aged well, started to get better throughout the year.” Risner’s relationship with Mims is particularly interesting because the two players are at dramatically different points in their careers. Mims is just 23 years old and entering his third NFL season. Risner, 31, is entering his eighth. “He is like a little brother to me. More than a little brother, he is a friend, and I want to see him succeed. I don’t want to let Mims down, I don’t want to let Ted down, I don’t want to let Joe down.” Risner says Mims isn’t simply a talented young tackle. He’s a student of the game. “During the season, we all ask Mims for the scouting report, for the injury report,” Risner said. “He knows all of this. He’s a football guy.” And Risner has been impressed by Mims’ willingness to recognize his own mistakes. “I think Mims is such a pro,” Risner said. “For me, it’s always seeing Mims for the positive things he does. Let’s go out there and take it one play at a time. During the game, it gets hectic. The way he is able to see his wrongs, I gained so much respect for him.” Mims believes that willingness to admit mistakes is essential to becoming the player he wants to be. “Once you’re vulnerable enough to understand where you need to grow, that’s when you become a good player,” Mims said. “Coach listed what we need to get better at, and we just had to go to work.” The admiration clearly goes both ways. “He’s one of the most selfless guys I’ve ever played with,” Mims said of Risner. “It’s always, ‘What can I do, how can I help you?’ That’s what I really like.” That relationship helped bring Risner back to Cincinnati. After joining the Bengals shortly before the beginning of last season, Risner eventually started 11 games. Cincinnati didn’t allow him to reach the open market this spring, re-signing him to a one-year contract before the start of free agency. According to Risner, Mims and Karras were among those pushing for his return. “For him to care enough to say something that kind and to want me back, I’ve never had teammates like Ted and Mims that really campaigned for me to come back,” Risner said. “And that’s why I wanted to come back. “I could have probably made more in free agency somewhere else, but this is where I wanted to be. You don’t have Mims, Ted Karras, OB [Orlando Brown] at other places.” The Bengals have rarely lacked offensive firepower during the Burrow era. The lingering question has been whether the five players up front could provide enough protection and a running game for that talent to reach its potential. For once, Cincinnati enters a season without having to introduce a collection of new offensive linemen to each other. They already know each other. They have struggled together. They have improved together. And, perhaps most importantly, they actually care about one another. “We went through not knowing each other, going through the worst times, then going through the best,” Mims said. “The sky’s the limit for us. “I’m very excited.” So is Cincinnati.
