title: Aaron Donald can earn $10 million if Rams win the Super Bowl
summary: The Los Angeles Rams brought back Aaron Donald on a one-year contract worth up to $30 million, and the initial estimate for his 2026 cap hit came in at $10 million with the potential to rise with incentives. However, the officially released cap numbers are much more tenable for 2026, while adding a significant number […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 08: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams adjusts his jersey as he looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Philadelphia Eagles at SoFi Stadium on October 08, 2023 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams brought back Aaron Donald on a one-year contract worth up to $30 million, and the initial estimate for his 2026 cap hit came in at $10 million with the potential to rise with incentives . However, the officially released cap numbers are much more tenable for 2026, while adding a significant number in the future when Donald could be back in retirement. Instead of $10 million, Donald’s cap hit will be $5.826 million, which is basically every cent of cap space that L.A. had left before he signed. Now Donald will carry a $17.925 million cap number in 2027, when Donald is not signed, and the contract has four void years. The deal has four void years, with dead money going out to 2030. Furthermore, Donald’s bonus works out like this: He gets $2.5 million if he plays 15% of the snaps and L.A. makes the playoffs (probable) $1.25 million if he’s active for a playoff berth $1.25 million if he’s active for the second round of the playoffs $2.5 million if the Rams go to the Super Bowl $2.5 million if the Rams win the Super Bowl DL Aaron Donald's 1-year, $20M #Rams Contract Cap Hits 2026: $5.8M 2027: $18M (void) Base Salary: $10M (gtd) Per-Game-Active: $10M $666,666 per game, max 15 $10M Incentive Package: pic.twitter.com/KJy8RDhIgt — Spotrac (@spotrac) September 3, 2026 The Rams have a lot of cap space in 2027, but they also have a lot of accounting to do with free agents. Basically all of their offensive line except for A.J. Jackson, plus Puka Nacua, Byron Young, Kobie Turner, and others. Will the Rams be able to eat $18 million for Donald? Will Donald want to play again in 2027 ? The Rams have an ability to carry 54 players on their roster through the first two weeks of the season thanks to Donald’s roster exemption provided by the league.

title: Is there chance Aaron Donald plays beyond 2026?
summary: The most likely answer is no. Aaron Donald is back with the Los Angeles Rams for the 2026 season, but everything about his return points toward this being a one-year comeback rather than the beginning of another multi-year chapter. Donald is 35 years old, has not played since the 2023 season and already walked away […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 07: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on from the sidelines prior to the start of an NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on January 07, 2024 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The most likely answer is no. Aaron Donald is back with the Los Angeles Rams for the 2026 season , but everything about his return points toward this being a one-year comeback rather than the beginning of another multi-year chapter. Donald is 35 years old, has not played since the 2023 season and already walked away from football once after a Hall of Fame career. He also signed a one-year contract with the Rams worth $20 million that can reach $30 million with incentives. The entire premise of his comeback appears to be centered around one goal: give Los Angeles another opportunity to win a championship. Still, there is a tiny possibility that 2026 changes everything. He already retired once because he felt complete with his career. After stepping away for more than two years, Donald has now put himself through a rigorous training process to determine whether he can still perform at a high level. The fact that he ultimately decided to return suggests that he believes there is one more great season left in him. The cleanest ending would be winning Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium and walking away as a champion for the second time. This is where the smallest possibility of a 2027 return becomes interesting. If Donald produces a massive statistical season in 2026, the conversation could look very different. Suppose he finishes the season with double-digit sacks, consistently wrecks games from the interior and looks like one of the NFL’s best defensive tackles. Suddenly, retirement might not feel quite as inevitable. And if the Rams fail to win Super Bowl LXI, Donald would have unfinished business. There is also a potentially important roster factor. Myles Garrett remains under contract, giving Los Angeles its defensive centerpiece beyond 2026. Meanwhile, Kobie Turner is scheduled to become an unrestricted free agent in 2027. If Turner leaves, the Rams could suddenly have a starting defensive tackle position available next to Poona Ford. That doesn’t mean Los Angeles would automatically bring Donald back. In fact, the team would probably prefer to continue developing its younger defensive linemen and maintain flexibility around Garrett. But if Donald is still playing at an elite level, the situation could be different. A lineup featuring Garrett on the edge, Donald and Ford inside could remain extremely dangerous. Donald also wouldn’t necessarily need to play an enormous percentage of snaps. At this stage of his career, a carefully managed workload could allow him to maximize his impact in passing situations. Ultimately, the chances of Donald playing beyond 2026 should be considered extremely small. The Rams acquired him for a championship push. Donald returned because he believes he has enough left to help them win another Super Bowl. And at 35, there is no guarantee that his body will want to go through this process again. If the Rams win Super Bowl LXI, it would be especially difficult to imagine Donald coming back. He would have achieved the exact goal that motivated his return. But if Los Angeles falls short and Donald somehow turns back the clock with a dominant statistical season, there could be one final question worth asking. Does Donald really want to walk away if he still believes he can dominate? The answer is probably yes. This is most likely a one-year comeback.

title: Is Klint Kubiak’s Raiders offense plug-and-play for any running back?
summary: Ashton Jeanty’s ankle ailment was certainly a cause for concern. The Las Vegas Raiders’ workhorse running back went down with the ankle injury back on August 23 during practice where he dove for a low pass and landed awkwardly. The ensuing silence and players and coaches kneeling was concerning, as was Jeanty unable to put […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Dylan Laube #23, Mike Washington Jr. #30 and Roman Hemby #37 of the Las Vegas Raiders warm up before a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Cardinals defeated the Raiders 27-14. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ashton Jeanty’s ankle ailment was certainly a cause for concern. The Las Vegas Raiders’ workhorse running back went down with the ankle injury back on August 23 during practice where he dove for a low pass and landed awkwardly. The ensuing silence and players and coaches kneeling was concerning, as was Jeanty unable to put weight on his right foot. But, in a turn of fortuitous events for the Silver & Black, it appears Jeanty avoided a serious injury. The team not placing Jeanty on injured reserve with a designated to return qualifier during cutdown day this past Sunday — when all 32 NFL teams needed to be at the mandated 53-man roster limit — portends to good things. (Not so much for 2026 Draft third-round pick Keyron Crawford who landed on season-ending injured reserve after suffering a serious ankle injury of his own in the third quarter of the preseason finale against the San Francisco 49ers last Thursday.) And Las Vegas rolling with a trio of tailbacks on the initial 53 (Jeanty, ravishing rookie Mike Washington Jr., and Dylan Laube) adds more fuel to the positivity fire regarding the starting running back. “He’s still on the mend and we’re still working to get him back. We got another week to assess how he’s going to look going into this first game, but we’re counting on him,” Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said regarding Jeanty. The injury scare produced a really good question for Las Vegas: Is Kubiak’s offense plug-and-play for any running back? The answer: A resounding no. Speed, vision, power ✅ Watch as @EricAllen619 dissects Mike Washington Jr.'s game tape in an all-new @Microsoft Breakdown ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/2A4oqpicB0 — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) May 13, 2026 While Kubiak’s ground game is philosophically based on the Shanahan-Kubiak (his father Gary, who himself is a disciple of the elder Shanahan, Mike as both a player and coach) wide-zone system — famous for turning mid- to late-round and even undrafted free agents into solid contributors — the scheme does require a highly specific skillset both mental and physical. Versatility Vortex Here’s the biggest rub when it comes to running backs in a Klint Kubiak offense: Alignment. Tailbacks don’t just line up in your standard I-formation behind the quarterback and fullback. Kubiak’s system heavily utilizes pre-snap motion, split-back sets, and formations shifts that call for running backs to line up as a perimeter receiver or even in the slot, before motion or shift calls them back to the traditional tailback spots in the backfield or keeps them out the outside/slot to run routes. Kubiak deploys running backs this way to create mismatches and to force defenses to show their hand with coverages, blitzes, etc. But that aspect above is what looms large as a play caller simply can’t put any tailback out wide or in the slot if they’re not effective route runners and receivers. They are high-volume targets in Kubiak’s system where running backs often finish in the top five in terms of targets and receptions. Jeanty, Washington, Laube, and practice-squad additions Dare Ogunbowale (veteran) Roman Hemby (undrafted free agent) bring the skillsets to be to do so in Kubiak’s Raiders backfield. Laube even showcased the slippery nature he provides as a receiving running back during the preseason — showcasing more confidence than he did the prior two coaching regimes. Then there’s all-important pass protection ability. In obvious passing downs, running backs in Kubiak’s offense need to handle the complexity of blocking. That means using the same snap-decision making running with the ball while protecting the quarterback as NFL defenses these days send a dizzying array of defensive fronts, blitzes (both simulated and actual), and the tailbacks must hold up physically against incoming defenders be they edge rushers, linebackers, or defensive backs. While Jeanty and Laube are “smaller” at 5-foot-8, 208 pounds and 5-foot-9 and 204 pounds, respectively, both have shown the ability to pass protect. And at 6-foot-2 and 228 pounds, Washington should be able to hang, as well. Dylan Laube takes it in for the TD and does his dance 🕺 LVvsHOU on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ASCka61RNq — NFL (@NFL) August 21, 2026 Run Requisites The Kubiak scheme very much relies on the one-cut decisiveness that’s been a staple alongside the zone blocking concepts that make it work. Thus, the core tenets of the outside/wide zone where running back’s can’t afford to dance or hesitate in the backfield are present. We’ve seen this in fleeting moments when Jeanty got carries in preseason action and most notably Washington’s decisiveness when the rookie plants and turns on the jets. In fact, we’ve seen the rookie exhibit the Three Bs — bang, bend, bounce — where he slices through the primary crease vertically, cuts back against the grain on backside lane, or even bounces it outside to the edge to out-run defenders. Kubiak, however, isn’t an obtuse coach or play caller. Putting his players in the best possible position during his tenure as the offensive coordinator for the Seattle Seahawks Super Bowl run last season resulted in him incorporating more gap and power schemes into his repertoire. And we’re seeing exactly that in Las Vegas. Washington arrived to the Silver & Black from a heavy gap system deployed in Arkansas and instead of plugging the talented tailback into the zone system, Kubiak has called toss and perimeter plays to help create space, give Washington ample time to mentally get in-tune, and force him to let blocks develop. A consistent and effective ground game is instrumental in the play-action concepts Kubiak plans to deploy with veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins (and prized No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza) success. Being able to run the ball for yards and aggressively sell a run to freeze defenders — facilitating to intermediate and deep shots downfield via the air attack — will be something to eye this season. It’ll take every part of the offense — offensive line, quarterback, running backs, wide receivers, and tight ends — to work in unison to make it click. And in those particular play action instances, you’ll get to see exactly the responsibility placed on the running back. Whether they remain in the backfield as a blocker, or an outlet target sneaking out of the backfield, or running specific routes as a receiving option, it’s a lot to handle. Which harkens on Kubiak’s system not being a plug-and-play type for running backs.
author: Ray Aspuria

title: Raiders defense: Kwity Paye’s ascension as complement to Maxx Crosby key
summary: With a salary cap in place, all 32 NFL teams operate with limited funds in any given year. And it’s that maximum limit in spending which puts return on investment (ROI) — a term usually reserved for the business world — under a bright spotlight. Such is the case for the Las Vegas Raiders. The […]
full_text: Former Hendricken player, Kwity Paye, of the Indianapolis Colts going up against Patriot TE Jonnu Smith in the first half as the New England Patriots hosts the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on Nov 6, 2022. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co With a salary cap in place, all 32 NFL teams operate with limited funds in any given year. And it’s that maximum limit in spending which puts return on investment (ROI) — a term usually reserved for the business world — under a bright spotlight. Such is the case for the Las Vegas Raiders. The team entered the 2026 offseason flush with cap space and general manager John Spytek certainly rolled up his sleeves, worked with his player personnel crew alongside head coach Klint Kubiak and his coaching staff, and went to work. Instead of bargain bin shopping on free agents like his initial season as the Silver & Black’s chief personnel man, Spytek and Co. spent the second-most coin in free agency this offseason at the tune of $308.157 million, according to Over The Cap . That sum finished just behind the Tennessee Titans who shelled out $317.962-plus million. That noted, the Raiders were also tops in total guarantees ($235-plus million) and full guarantees ($201-plus million). Hence, the focus on ROI. We’ll focus particularly one one specific free agent: Kwity Paye. Las Vegas signed the former Indianapolis Colt to the second-most expensive free agent contract it doled out with a three-year, $48 million pact. Spending that kind of coin on a pass rusher requires confidence in high returns and Paye becoming the complementary presence opposite elite edge Maxx Crosby is integral to the Raiders’ desire to succeed in Year 1 under Kubiak and beyond. Maxx Crosby turns 29 today 🦅🎂 The #Raiders star edge rusher recently came in at No. 24 in NFL’s Top 100. pic.twitter.com/i4cdfnc570 — Nick Walters (@nickwalt) August 22, 2026 Just as how fleeting the Raiders responsible resource allocation has been, so has the presence opposite of the team’s premiere edge rusher. The last time the Silver & Black deployed a complementary piece was in the 2021 and 2023 seasons, years where Yannick Ngakoue roared off the other side for 10 sacks in ’21and then Malcolm Koonce who had a breakout campaign with eight sacks in ’23. Koonce very much remains as part of the team (inking a one-year, $11.04 million contract this offseason) and is trying to recapture his 2023 form after a torn ACL suffered in 2024. Which brings us back to the Raiders’ newly-inked and rich edge rusher. Paye Day At a sturdy 6-foot-3 and 265 pounds, Paye was the the 21st overall prospect taken by the Colts in the 2021 NFL Draft out of Michigan and was expected to have explosive testing numbers at the NFL Combine that year. However, much of that occurred at the Wolverines’ Pro Day where Paye clocked in a 4.57-second 40-yard dash time (for comparison, Crosby hit 4.66 at the 2019 combine) to go along with a 35.5-inch vertical jump and 36 bench press reps. After five years in Indianapolis, Las Vegas came calling and offered both a nifty pay day and a scheme that enticed Paye. “The scheme is something that really drew me to come here. And just Robbie (Leonard) being the DC (defenisve coordinator) and wanting to come out here and play with these guys,” Paye noted in early August after one of the Raiders’ training camp practices. “Yeah, I think for me, I just got to put everything on the line,” Paye added. “Going into my sixth year playing a lot of football. I feel like there’s still a lot more for me to give. I’m just excited for this defense, this scheme. It’s different from last year and I’m just excited. Robbie probably is going to dial it up.” Dialing it up from Leonard’s play calling and player development and Paye is instrumental too how the Raiders defense sinks or swims this coming season. While Paye hasn’t eclipsed the 10-sack mark yet (his highest output was 8.5 in 2023), he does have the size, power, and athleticism to be a force against the run and pass. He’s totaled 37 tackles for loss alongside 30.5 sacks, 50 quarterback hits, four forced fumbles, and 123 solo tackles in his career, according to Pro Football Reference (PFR). PFR also charted Paye with 97 pressures and 44 hurries over his five years in the league so far. Paye has the skillset and production to make teams rue double-teaming and focusing all the attention on Crosby. And that’s simply what a lot of opponents did against the Raiders. Occupy Crosby with as many offensive lineman and chip blocks from tight ends and running backs, and run the play to the opposite side. Sure, Crosby still blows up plays, but Paye becoming a force to be reckoned with on the opposite side is sorely needed by the Silver & Black. Better use 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀 protection. Get to know Kwity Paye ➡️ https://t.co/s28CxGVHit | 📺NFL+ pic.twitter.com/ipEZhXKzxy — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) March 14, 2026 Flexible Fit Because of his size, speed, and strength combination, Paye provides Leonard a defender who can line up in a variety of spots to maximize output. Leonard is expected to run a fluid defense that shifts between the traditional 3-4 and 4-3 alignments while mixing in tricks of the trade he learned from Seattle Seahawks head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald, Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, and former Raiders defensive boss (and current Pittsburgh Steelers DC) Patrick Graham. Paye has the physicality and athleticism to set the edge to stymie the run and rushing the passer from the edge or sliding inside to provide bite as an interior rusher. “It’s been really fun. I can play everywhere really. Robbie knows that, so it’s been good to play some 3-technique, play some Big End, play some SAM linebacker,” Paye said. “And then versatility with other players too, like Quay (Walker), who”s playing the Dime, the WILL, and the SAM as well. It just gives Robbie more options in his play calling and he’ll feel comfortable calling the call.” The deployment by Leonard and Paye’s production will go a long way into ROI and justifying the financial investment the Raiders made in the 27-year-old defender. Paye tied his career-low in terms of sacks with just four in his final season with the Colts (he also had four as a rookie) and is looking to bounce back with his new squad. But with Crosby rushing from the opposite side, the presence of linebackers Walker and Nakobe Dean (both adept at rushing the passer on blitzes), alongside the coverage on the back end, there’s a lot of moving parts there but once it clicks (it must), Leonard’s defense has the opportunity to right the wrongs from year’s past. “Obviously, I love how fast our defense started and how great of a job they did on third down, in the red zone,” Kubiak said of what he saw from Leonard’s group in the preseason finale. “I thought our coaches have done an excellent job. I look forward to going and playing these games with our starters for a full four quarters and then playing a full game together. Offense, defense and special teams complementing each other. That’s the goal, to get all three phases playing at a high level.” It’s been a long time since complementary football was synonymous with the Raiders.
author: Ray Aspuria

title: What did the preseason show us about the Las Vegas Raiders
summary: The 2026 NFL preseason ended for the (1-3) Las Vegas Raiders with an 18-12 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. Over the course of three preseason games, we have seen enough of a sample size to get a decent idea of who they are. What they do well and where they will struggle. Who are […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 27: Treydan Stukes #31, Dalton Johnson #43 and Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders leave the field after the team's 18-12 loss in a preseason game to the San Francisco 49ers at Allegiant Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL preseason ended for the (1-3) Las Vegas Raiders with an 18-12 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. Over the course of three preseason games, we have seen enough of a sample size to get a decent idea of who they are. What they do well and where they will struggle. Who are the Raiders The Raiders are a run heavy team and will go as far as their run game will take them. In the offseason a commitment was made to improving the offensive line and so far they have received a legitimate return. Rick Dennison and his staff have improved the run blocking significantly from top to bottom. Raiders run game 📈 Watch them run trap this year compared to last year pic.twitter.com/YIMgVytVMX — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) August 28, 2026 Lanes to run not only exist, but have led to Mike Washington Jr amassing an impressive seven yards per carry throughout the entire preseason. Great downfield blocking from receivers has allowed the run game to move the ball up and down the field. The passing game remains a work in progress. The Raiders excel in the short passing game and have sparingly had some success in the intermediate. Throwing the ball downfield has only been attempted a handful of times and worked a couple times. What can you expect on defense Schematically, a more aggressive defense is what defensive coordinator Rob Leonard is bringing to the table. Lots of disguise in coverages and surely his blitz package is extensive based off the alignments and personnel. Better tackling and fundamentals will be a benchmark to keep watch for. Maxx Crosby has yet to take the field against an opponent in 2026. All accounts suggest the burst is back and he is every bit the menace and defensive edge force we know him to be. His impact will be a massive help to the entire defense and take pressure off the young guys. The young defensive backs are going to be really good once the game slows down and they lock in. As a whole, the defensive backfield appears to have recovered and grown from a horrendous showing against the Cardinals in Week 1. Eric Stokes, Taron Johnson and Darian Porter appear very comfortable in the scheme. With a pass rush and provided they locate the football when thrown, they will get their hands on the ball. Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker are going to make plays for this defense. When they finally get a chance to work with Crosby on a play-by-play basis good things are going to happen. Where they stand in week 1 Heading into the regular season the Raiders are a work in progress. Rome wasn’t built in a day and neither will this roster be built in one offseason. Progress has certainly been achieved and better days are on the horizon. The possibility of going worst to first appears slightly outside the range of an ICBM, but still exists should things begin to click. Consistency is king for a reason, usually a team needs around half to three quarters of a season to gel completely. For a team with as much turnover as the Raiders, that’s not conducive to winning.

title: The Las Vegas Raiders youth movement: Generation- D
summary: When Las Vegas Raiders general manager John Spytek overhauled nearly his entire defensive corps with rookies, a statement was being made. The Raiders chose to focus on their own young group of talent and develop them in-house rather than keep overpaying free agents and hoping for the best. He definitely got some signs of promise […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 27: Eddy Pineiro #18 of the San Francisco 49ers kicks a 54-yard field goal as Buddy Johnson #59, Cian Slone #48, Brandon Cleveland #90 and Gary Smith III #75 of the Las Vegas Raiders try to block it in the fourth quarter of their preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The 49ers defeated the Raiders 18-12. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Las Vegas Raiders general manager John Spytek overhauled nearly his entire defensive corps with rookies, a statement was being made. The Raiders chose to focus on their own young group of talent and develop them in-house rather than keep overpaying free agents and hoping for the best. He definitely got some signs of promise out of this draft season. Let’s take a look at some of the productive defensive rookies of the preseason. One starter and three rotators Higher draft selections come with higher expectations and greater potential than others. Grading rookies is more about gauging the frequency of flash plays along with the consistency of elevated play. Undrafted free agents have a tougher row to hoe must hit the scene and play at a level no one can deny. Treydan Stukes – 2nd Round: Stukes has all but officially snatched Isaiah Palo Mao’s starting free safety spot. Initially, there were concerns as he needed some time to earn his place amongst the ones on defense. Stukes has learned what it is he’s supposed to do and is beginning to play faster and faster. Stukes has the throwback size and elite speed to cover all kinds of ground and make plays. As his confidence has grown so has his play. Keyron Crawford – 3rd Round: Crawford can be summed up in one word: RAW. Crawford has limitless potential and only knows one speed. Learning to harness the speed for when he needs it while playing under control will help him transcend into possibly an elite athlete off the edge. Jermod McCoy – 4th Round: McCoy has shown why he is so highly regarded every time he takes the field. His mirror technique is nearly flawless. He stays in phase and has been removing his assignment from the quarterback’s option list. Watching him knock off the rust and absolutely strap up receivers has been a thing of beauty to behold. Locating the football in the air is a skill that, once he acquires and perfects, the sky is the limit for McCoy. Hezekiah Masses – 5th Round: Masses is another of the California Golden Bears’ finest. Former Cal head coach Justin Wilcox has produced a plethora of excellent defensive backs during his expired tenure in Berkeley, Ca; Masses fits right in with the rest of them. Quality depth pieces Cian Slone – UDFA: Slone plays like he’s Maxx Crosby’s little brother out there. The former North Carolina State Wolfpack outside linebacker is pure dynamite every time he steps out on the field. His talents appear to have earned him a roster spot with a contributing role on defense. As an edge, Slone isn’t the biggest or the fastest, but at six-foot-three and 238 pounds, he is out-hustling everyone, winning reps and making plays with a unique blend of technique and maximization of his abilities. He hasn’t made the team yet, but one would imagine he should soon. Dalton Johnson – 5th Round: Johnson has been a hellhound on special teams and is slowly coming along in terms of being an NFL strong safety. Johnson has made great play after play on special teams. Displaying amazing kick coverage and open-field tackling. As a safety, he will be a depth piece behind Jeremy Chinn and Isaiah Palo Mao. Practice squad Brandon Cleveland – 7th Round: Cleveland is an interesting player who you have to be able to watch football away from the ball to see how he is getting down. Some players eat double teams; others find a way to survive them. Cleveland survives NFL double teams but dominates single blockers. Cleveland has the look of a player who will find himself on the practice squad for a year, maybe two, while he refines his hand fighting and gets better at fending off double teams.

title: Doubt in Dolphins; Can Miami prove everyone wrong?
summary: There are not many believers in the 2026 version of the Miami Dolphins in the national media. Ever since the hiring of new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and the subsequent mass exodus of talent across the roster, the talk has been more about Miami’s dead cap situation and the possibility of the organization “earning” the […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - AUGUST 20: Head coach Jeff Hafley of the Miami Dolphins speask to the media during training camp at Baptist Health Training Complex on August 20, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are not many believers in the 2026 version of the Miami Dolphins in the national media. Ever since the hiring of new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and the subsequent mass exodus of talent across the roster, the talk has been more about Miami’s dead cap situation and the possibility of the organization “earning” the number one overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft than the team possibly winning actual football games on the field this upcoming season. In Week One, Miami will travel to Las Vegas to take on the Raiders — a team that won three games in 2025 and wound up picking first in the 2026 NFL Draft themselves. Still, heading into that game, the Dolphins are considered the underdogs according to most sportsbooks. In fact, in most places, the Raiders are favored by at least three points, with some sites favoring them by four points or more. Count the talking heads at NFL Network as those with the mindset that the Dolphins will be bad — like, really bad — in 2026. In fact, against the Raiders, not a single person has picked Miami to win that game, or even cover the spread. NFL Network makes picks for Week 1, Dolphins at Raiders pic.twitter.com/XML8k3Jnpf — Joe Schad (@schadjoe) September 3, 2026 In 2025, the Raiders defense gave up an average of 25.4 points per game — the 8th most in the National Football League. As you can see above, Brandon Perna thinks the Dolphins will score exactly three points against that defense. At the end of the day, what Dan Parr, Kevin Patra, Brooke Cersosimo and others think probably doesn’t matter all that much to the folks inside the buildings in Miami Gardens. The Dolphins can’t control the pessimistic predictions coming from outside of the organization. They can only control what happens when they take the field against the Raiders. And right now, seeing nearly every analyst around the league disrespect them should provide all the motivation Miami needs. The doubters have spoken. Now it’s up to the Dolphins to answer — not with words, but with toughness, heart… And hopefully, a win.

title: Patriots mailbag: What comes next with Christian Gonzalez?
summary: Football is less than a week away as the New England Patriots get set to open the 2026 NFL season with a Super Bowl rematch against the Seattle Seahawks. Enough is said, so let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What do you think is a reasonable contract for the Patriots and Gonzalez to come […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots lines up during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the Houston Texans at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Football is less than a week away as the New England Patriots get set to open the 2026 NFL season with a Super Bowl rematch against the Seattle Seahawks. Enough is said, so let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What do you think is a reasonable contract for the Patriots and Gonzalez to come to in terms of total salary, total guaranteed, guaranteed at signing, and signing bonus and any other parameters you want to throw in? – New England Guy I’ve heard some team reporters say Gonzo has essentially no leverage. Is that really true? Can he realistically hold out, and what happens if he refuses to practice? The only meaningful leverage I’ve heard is that if he doesn’t play by Week 10, his contract and fifth-year option could toll a year—bad for him if he wants to get paid sooner. – Maye The Force Be With You By his own words, Christian Gonzalez has not committed to playing in the Patriots’ season opener Wednesday night. Mike Vrabel, meanwhile, expects “every player that is healthy and under contract to practice and to play.” If the cornerback doesn’t suit up, this saga reaches a new level. As you stated, Gonzalez needs to play six games this year to accrue a year of service time. A holdout would prevent him from making progress toward free agency while then seemingly increasing the odds of a trade next offseason. I still do not believe it gets to that point. I’d continue to guess that Gonzalez plays Wednesday night, as the two sides will continue to try to get a deal done before then. As for the structure, I would continue to use Devon Witherspoon’s deal (below) as a framework, with a slight bump: Total value: $132 million AAV: $33 million Guaranteed money: $101 million Guaranteed at signing: $59 million My on-topic contribution: Do you see a world in which the O-line turns from a liability to a reasonable strength, making this a truly elite offense? (I do.) – ed.liebfried I do too, Ed. Will Campbell is healthy and had an overall solid training camp. He should take a step forward in Year 2, in addition to getting center Jared Wilson back at his natural position. The addition of veteran Alijah Vera-Tucker should make both of the second-year linemen’s lives easier as well. There are plenty of projections there, but they have the talent and potential to be an offensive line that at least ranks in the top half of the league. Especially with the Seahawks game in mind, have the Pats done enough (adding AVT, Gilliam and blocking TE’s) to protect Maye and give him the time to succeed? – Ricky Hot Pants As we discussed above, the offensive line group should take a step forward with the internal development of the young players and addition of Alijah Vera-Tucker. Additions like Reggie Gilliam should also allow the Patriots to play and take advantage of more heavy personnel groupings than they did in the Super Bowl, where they lived in 11 personnel. Those improvements should help the offense against Seattle’s four-man rush — which shined in the Super Bowl — and in the Patriots’ run game. From there, New England will need better answers against Mike Macdonald’s pressure looks this time around. In addition to the four-man rush, the biggest issue against Seattle in the Super Bowl was the Patriots’ lack of answers against the Seahawks’ pressure packages. New England failed to either have “hot” options available to Drake Maye or correctly adjust the protection pre-snap. The Patriots spent much of this offseason weaponizing Maye’s mind as he enters Year 2 in Josh McDaniels’ system, hoping to avoid similar issues moving forward. “I think just more comfort in what we are doing, more command, more understanding to be able to operate and get us into the best plays,” Vrabel said about Maye’s improvements from the end of last season. Do you think the Pats OLine could be better with Roten starting at Center to begin the year and start Wilson after a few games after he gets a little more familiar with the Center position in the NFL? – sjamesbossports I do not. I think Wilson is a good center prospect and Van Roten fits in better at guard whereas Ben Brown is likely the backup center. I’m sorry but adding 10 new players after cut down day, causes me to think the Patriots, scouting, drafting and player development is not good enough. 10 new players, suggest the had the wrong players in camp. Your thoughts? – Patriot in Chicago To me, it comes down to two main things: injuries and free agency. The Patriots are starting the year without OT Marcus Bryant, TE Julian Hill, RB Terrell Jennings, OLB Harold Landry III and ST Brenden Schooler. Each player was expected to assume a starting or backup role and deepen the roster. As for free agency, they did not hit on the middle class of free agents this year with guys like Mike Brown, Kindle Vildor and K.J. Britt compared to the likes of Khyiris Tonga, Jack Gibbens and K’Lavon Chaisson last season. What are your thoughts about Ponder being a starter week1 as DE coming from nowhere last year ? – 7i165 I am a fan of Elijah Ponder. He’s a great athlete off the edge and had some really strong moments against some of the best tackles in football last season. But, going from a rotational player who logged just 215 defensive snaps to a full-time, three-down starter is a major ask for a 24-year old that was an undrafted free agent. We will see if he is ready. I have heard next to nothing about Reggie Gilliam. What I have heard is more like the theoretical value of having a true fullback on the roster again. But did he look good in camp? Did he play in preseason? Is there any indication of how the offense has evolved with his addition? – NEsuper It was tough to evaluate Gilliam as the team really managed his workload this summer to help him deal with past injuries that have nagged him. There isn’t much concern that that will affect him during the season as he has been one of the league’s best fullbacks for multiple years. As we hinted on above, his arrival will allow the team to find more success in heavier, two-back personnel groupings. Last season, New England averaged just 3.1 yards and a negative EPA/rush in those looks. Buffalo, meanwhile, averaged 4.9 yards per rush and nearly 9.0 yards per pass with Gilliam on the field. He should make life easier for the whole offense. Who has been the biggest surprise (positive or negative) from Training Camp/Preseason that casual fans should pay more attention to as the season begins? – LandenPatz1 For the casual fans, it’s been pretty striking to see the turnover on special teams. Among the Patriots players who played over 100 snaps on the kick or punt team last season, they have lost: Brenden Schooler (NFI), Jack Gibbens, Marte Mapu, Jahlani Tavai, Jack Westover, Anfernee Jennings, Alex Austin and K’Lavon Chaisson. Elijah Ponder was also part of that group and could take a reduced role due to his standing on the defensive depth chart. That is massive turnover in the kicking game — which doesn’t even count Bryce Baringer’s injury — that has been replaced by rookies and some recent waiver claims. While special teams is often overlooked, it can make a big impact in a game. “The trust factor is what it comes down to in the kicking game because those kick returns, punt returns, a block punt, those usually lose you games. If you give up return touchdowns, and conversely if you hit them. those help you win and lose games,” VP of player personnel Ryan Cowden said. “So that’s why it’s such a vital piece of the game and you do sometimes want to rely on guys who’ve been there done that, but inevitably you have to lean into these young players.” Why do you think the Pats didn’t keep Saunders, even on the PS? Ball-hawking…

(Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images A spot on the New England Patriots’ practice squad has changed hands. The organization announced the signing of safety Elliott Davison on Thursday afternoon. To make room for the free agent, defensive tackle Jalen Hunt has been released from the 17-man group . Davison, 24, entered the NFL as an undrafted rookie out of UTSA in 2025. The 6-foot, 200-pound former Roadrunners defensive back spent his first regular season on the practice squad of the New Orleans Saints and was retained on a futures contract in January. After seeing 141 snaps between defense and special teams during August preseason action, which included one start in the secondary, he cleared waivers at the league’s 53-man roster deadline last weekend. Hunt, 25, had been among a series of additions to New England’s initial practice squad as the calendar turned to September. Prior to then, the 6-foot-2, 310-pound undrafted defensive lineman logged his rookie training camp with the Jacksonville Jaguars and went unclaimed at the cutdown. Hunt spent three seasons at Michigan State before transferring to Cincinnati for the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. He appeared in 48 games during his collegiate career while notching 48 tackles and 3.5 sacks. The current practice squad in Foxborough includes running backs Hassan Haskins and Lan Larison, wide receivers Kyle Dixon and Cameron Dorner, tight end Shane Zylstra, offensive linemen Jake Kubas and Jacob Rizy, defensive linemen Eric Gregory and Jeremiah Pharms Jr., linebackers Jose Ramirez, K.J. Britt and LB Riley Wilson, defensive backs Kindle Vildor and Mike Brown, plus punter Mitch Wishnowsky. At capacity, the Patriots also carry an exemption for German offensive tackle Lorenz Metz through the NFL’s International Player Pathway.

full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 07: TreVeyon Henderson #32 of the New England Patriots arrives to New England Patriots training camp on August 6, 2026 at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots were back on the practice fields on Thursday for a bonus day of work ahead of Week 1. Running back TreVeyon Henderson remained sidelined after the second-year back suffered an ankle injury early last week. Henderson was again present in the locker room and walking without a limp, but continues to work through the rehabilitation process. Elsewhere on the roster, recently claimed tight end Cameron Latu was again a non-participant in addition to offensive lineman Ben Brown. Brown, who was released on Monday before re-signing with the team on Tuesday as part of a logistical move, is nursing an injury he suffered in the preseason opener. The Patriots donned shells on the practice fields as the focus on Thursday was first and second downs with preparation continuing for opening night against the Seahawks. “We’ll go at with some speed today,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “We only get 14 padded practices through 17 weeks. 11 of which have to be in the first 11 weeks. So we’ll be in the shells. We’ll have to start to learn how to practice with shells on without shoulder pads which I think is something that good teams know how to do. “I think that they can go with speed and it’s not a jog through. There’s speed but there’s no collisions. But there has to be contact. It’s practice. We have to get these reps for first and second down. So, I’m looking forward to seeing where we’re at here going into the first and second down offense.” New England will have three more practices this week on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday before they leave for Seattle on Monday afternoon. The Super Bowl rematch is then set for Wednesday at 8:20 p.m. ET to kickoff the 2026 NFL season.

title: Patriots rookie found out he made the roster via Instagram
summary: Unlike 37 of his teammates, Quintayvious Hutchins was not asked to return his iPad ahead of the NFL roster cutdown deadline on Sunday. The New England Patriots had decided to keep the rookie outside linebacker on their 53-man roster. They just never actually told him. One of the quirks of cutdown day, after all, is […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Quintayvious Hutchins #45 of the New England Patriots lines up against the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL preseason football game at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Unlike 37 of his teammates , Quintayvious Hutchins was not asked to return his iPad ahead of the NFL roster cutdown deadline on Sunday. The New England Patriots had decided to keep the rookie outside linebacker on their 53-man roster. They just never actually told him. One of the quirks of cutdown day, after all, is that only players to get released are typically informed of their fate. Others are not, which might come as a surprise to first-year players such as Hutchins. He instead found out that he had made the team by scrolling through social media. “[An] Instagram post, when they posted the 53-man roster, that’s how I really found out,” he told the media at his New locker this week. “I saw the 53-man roster and was like, ‘Oh damn, I really made it.’” Having spent his entire five-year college career at Boston College, Hutchins made the move to Foxborough as the 247th overall pick in this year’s draft. Given his late-round status and the competition in the room, his spot on the eventual roster was not guaranteed. However, the 23-year-old had a solid training camp and saw a steady uptick in quality reps along the Patriots’ defensive edge. This, plus a preseason performance that saw him register eight tackles and a sack as well as three special teams takedowns, set the stage for him to ultimately make the team. Together with Dre’Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder and fellow rookie Gabe Jacas, he now is one of only four outside linebackers on the team. With that first step now taken, Hutchins is already looking ahead. “The job is not done. Continue to prove myself to earn a role on the team and just be dominant every chance I get,” he said. “You have to come in, work, keep your head up, and keep going.”

title: Saints surprisingly waive two players with injury settlements
summary: The New Orleans Saints are still working out their roster, and until game time in Week 1, there will be changes. That could be on the current 53-man roster, the practice squad, or even the current players on season-ending IR. Those injured players are the topic of today’s news. In an interesting decision, to say […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are still working out their roster, and until game time in Week 1, there will be changes. That could be on the current 53-man roster, the practice squad, or even the current players on season-ending IR. Those injured players are the topic of today’s news. In an interesting decision, to say the least, the Saints reached injury settlements with RB Devin Neal and EDGE Michael Heldman, sending them both to waivers. The #Saints have waived both RB Devin Neal and DE Michael Heldman with injury settlement pic.twitter.com/tfyhpsHjq9 — Tina Howell (@TinaM_Howell) September 3, 2026 Starting with what an injury settlement is: it is a way for the Saints to move on from these players and avoid using resources on players who were not going to make the roster. The players get paid for the time they would have been out and, in turn, become free agents. The team can re-sign both players once, after the injury settlement period is complete, plus three weeks (which is the rule). The salary cap also saves the team money by going in this direction. Now, onto the players themselves, it hurts that this is happening with Neal and Heldman. For Neal, he was on the outside of the RB competition due to injuries, but when he played, it was really positive. The hamstring could not heal, as we all saw in the game against the Los Angeles Rams. Still, he could have been a nice long-term RB option for the Saints. The Heldman move made even less sense. This move suggests he was unlikely to make the roster, likely due to the Saints’ depth at EDGE, but his potential was evident. He made plays throughout the preseason and showed flashes of becoming a really good pass rusher. So, when he did get injured and was ruled out for the year, the Saints got a bit lucky because they could keep him on the roster for the entire year without having to move on from him due to space constraints. This is why the move to reach an injury settlement with him is risky. If the Saints can bring back these two players after the settlements are finalized, then great; if not, we could look back on this move as a regrettable one.

title: Saints rookie report: Preseason Recap
summary: WR Jordyn Tyson Did not play in preseason. DT Christen Miller It wasn’t surprising that Christen Miller was a standout in preseason, but it was a bit of a shock just how important he was to this defense. Miller was the Saints’ best run defender and dealt with double teams well. He dealt with some […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 15: Jeremiah Wright #65 of the New Orleans Saints against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Caesars Superdome on August 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images WR Jordyn Tyson Did not play in preseason. DT Christen Miller It wasn’t surprising that Christen Miller was a standout in preseason, but it was a bit of a shock just how important he was to this defense. Miller was the Saints’ best run defender and dealt with double teams well. He dealt with some injuries throughout the preseason, and those are something to keep in mind, but it was clear he did everything he could to get back on the field. The Saints are going to have a hard time keeping him off the field this season. TE Oscar Delp Delp did not have a great preseason and was unable to stay healthy. He is still dealing with his injury, and his status for Week 1 is unknown. He’s still developing as a TE and will need time in general to make a significant impact on offense. OG Jeremiah Wright Wright was another one of the more developmental players in the Saints’ draft class, but unlike Delp, he played every game and improved each time. By the end of preseason, Wright looked like a standout player on the offensive line and looked solid in both run blocking. The Saints will not start Wright in Week 1, but just like they did with rookies last season, if Cesar Ruiz is struggling, Kellen Moore may not waste time making a change. WRs Bryce Lance and Barion Brown Game three against the Cowboys was an excellent performance by Lance and Brown, proving how important they are to the offense. Lance’s blocking was incredible, Brown’s athleticism made him a threat each time he was on the field, and Moore used them perfectly. This was the story of really the entire preseason, but game three was the cherry on top. DB Lorenzo Styles Jr. Another injured rookie, Styles Jr. will be starting the season on IR. Missing the first four games is never good for a rookie, but Styles Jr. was likely going to only play on special teams anyway. His preseason was a bit up and down. Styles Jr. made some nice plays but also got beat in coverage. Clearly, he was not ready to start on defense, but as I mentioned, that was never the plan for him this season. CB TJ Hall Jr. Hall Jr. did not survive the 53-man roster cuts, but was brought back to the practice squad. Hopefully, the rookie can stay there and develop this season. OT Mason Murphy Everyone, say hello to the Saints’ new rookie! Yes, one of the team’s signings after the 53-man roster deadline was former Chicago Bears offensive lineman Mason Murphy. He went undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, but the Saints clearly liked him as a depth piece for this offensive line. Murphy was also Wright’s teammate at Auburn and can step in at either tackle or center for the Saints if needed.

title: NY Giants’ Cam Skattebo addresses rumors of rift with John Harbaugh
summary: Cam Skattebo on Thursday put to bed the social media-created idea that there is a rift between the running back and New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh. “There’s that video going around of me and Harbaugh on the sidelines of ”not liking” what I said or whatever,“ Skattebo acknowledged during an appearance on ‘Up […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Cam Skattebo on Thursday put to bed the social media-created idea that there is a rift between the running back and New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh . “There’s that video going around of me and Harbaugh on the sidelines of ”not liking” what I said or whatever,“ Skattebo acknowledged during an appearance on ‘Up & Adams’ with Kay Adams. “I think the conversation was just less of a happy, joking conversation. It was just kind of a more serious conversation. It wasn’t nothing negative or nothing positive. There was just no emotion that needed to be shown.” Skattebo went on to explain that the conversation was about whether it was “more messed up” to knee the ball at the opponent’s 1-yard line or to go ahead and score. The Giants had quarterback Jake Haener take a knee to end their 23-6 preseason victory over the New York Jets. Skattebo said Harbaugh is “awesome.” “He’s just tough, man. He’s keeping the way you need to coach football in football,” Skattebo said. “A lot of the guys they get all this money and they get older and they don’t want to go out and practice hard and be in full pads every day. “He’s brought this culture where we’re gonna practice, we’re gonna practice for every minute that we’re allowed to … and we’re gonna do it in pads as much as we possibly can because that’s how football is played. “I really enjoy that.” Adams asked Skattebo about Harbaugh’s “infectious disease” comment after Skattebo got into a practice skirmish with defensive teammates. “Me and Harbs, we’re on the same page. We love each other. We’re awesome,” Skattebo said. “Me and him talk every single day. There’s no bad blood between us.” Skattebo said the remark was meant to illustrate that “what I did was infectious, an infectious disease, in that moment. Not that I’m an infectious disease person … I don’t think it was anything that was a big deal.” "Me and [John Harbaugh], we're on the same page, we love each other." 📝 🤔🙃😊☺️ pic.twitter.com/CcvRanquq3 — Kay Adams (@heykayadams) September 3, 2026

Neal was one of two former Giants signed to the practice by the Raiders, with the other being Azeez Ojulari. Neal, the No. 7 overall selection by the Giants in the 2022 NFL Draft, was let go […]
full_text: Evan Neal | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Evan Neal has a new employer, landing on the practice squad of the Las Vegas Raiders on Thursday. Neal was one of two former Giants signed to the practice by the Raiders , with the other being Azeez Ojulari. Neal, the No. 7 overall selection by the Giants in the 2022 NFL Draft, was let go by the Giants in the recent cutdown to the 53-man roster limit. He played in just 29 games with 27 starts for the Giants, and goes down as a massive draft bust. The Giants moved him from right tackle to guard last season, but he never played in a regular-season game at that position. Ojulari, an edge defender, was a second-round pick by then-GM Dave Gettleman in 2021. He had 8.0 sacks as a rookie, but injuries marred his next three seasons with New York as he never played in more than 11 games. Ojularie signed with the Philadelphia Eagles as a free agent last season, but appeared in just three games.

title: NY Giants sign LB Malik Harrison
summary: The New York Giants have signed veteran linebacker Malik Harrison to their practice squad. Harrison is a seven-year veteran who’s a very familiar face for head coach John Harbaugh. Harrison was originally a third-round pick out of Ohio State by the Baltimore Ravens in the 2020 NFL Draft. Harrison played for the Ravens until 2024, […]
full_text: The Giants add a former 3rd round linebacker to their practice squad Malik Harrison at linebacker for the Baltimore Ravens | Getty Images The New York Giants have signed veteran linebacker Malik Harrison to their practice squad. Harrison is a seven-year veteran who’s a very familiar face for head coach John Harbaugh. Harrison was originally a third-round pick out of Ohio State by the Baltimore Ravens in the 2020 NFL Draft. Harrison played for the Ravens until 2024, and signed with the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025. While Harrison signed a two-year $10 million contract with the Steelers, he spent most of last year on injured reserve after injuring his knee in Week 1. He was released by the Steelers in final cutdowns this summer. Harrison has great size at 6-foot-3, 247 pounds, with good athleticism, and 43 starts in 87 appearances. It remains to be seen if Harrison will be on the field for the Giants, but he’s been an NFL caliber player in his career. The Giants released UDFA defensive tackle Ben Barten to open the spot on their practice squad.

title: NY Giants’ Darius Slayton aiming to outplay expectations again
summary: Wide receiver Darius Slayton finds himself in an all-too-familiar place with the New York Giants entering the 2026 NFL season. For the fourth time since being a fifth-round pick by the Giants in the 2019 NFL Draft, Slayton is being doubted and having to prove to a new coaching staff that he can add value […]
full_text: Darius Slayton | Getty Images Wide receiver Darius Slayton finds himself in an all-too-familiar place with the New York Giants entering the 2026 NFL season. For the fourth time since being a fifth-round pick by the Giants in the 2019 NFL Draft, Slayton is being doubted and having to prove to a new coaching staff that he can add value to the offense. “So, anytime there’s new people, there’s going to be that,” Slayton said recently. “Just for me, I’ve just been fortunate to be here for four staffs. So, I don’t take it personally. I understand that you have to show and prove yourself whenever there’s new. So, that’s what I plan to do this year.” When the Giants drafted Slayton in the fifth round out of Auburn in 2019, Pat Shurmur was the coach and Dave Gettleman the GM. He came with a reputation as a fast guy who had a hard time catching the ball. He played his way onto the field and caught 48 passes for a team-high 740 yards. In 2020, Joe Judge was the coach. Slayton caught 50 balls for a team-high 751 yards. In 2022, Joe Schoen became the GM and Brian Daboll the coach. They were clearly not Slayton fans. He was inactive Week 1 and did not get a target or reception until Week 4. He still caught 46 passes for a team-high 724 yards. He eventually earned a three-year, $36 million contract from Schoen. Following the trade of Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals in the offseason, the 29-year-old Slayton is the longest-tenured Giant. “I think maybe contrary to common belief, studies would suggest that I’ve done more good than bad,” Slayton said. “Otherwise, I probably would have been gone with three different people coming here and evaluating me, but it is what it is.” Now, with John Harbaugh as head coach, Slayton again finds himself needing to prove his worth. In the days leading up to cutdowns to the 53-man roster, Slayton’s name came up as a potential trade or cut candidate. Slayton has heard that before. “It’s not the first time, probably won’t be the last time,” Slayton said. “But I really don’t pay it too much mind, honestly. I just take it day by day.” The Giants’ wide receiver room is, of course, anchored by Malik Nabers. After that, there are several players who will vie for snaps and targets. There is Odell Beckham Jr. Harbaugh has already promised that Beckham will play, not spectate as a nostalgia act. There is third-round pick Malachi Fields, who was impressive all summer and has a skill set none of the other receivers have. There is Darnell Mooney, who is similar to Slayton but has 1,00-yard and 900-yard receiving seasons on his resume that Slayton can’t match. Braxton Berrios is on the practice squad, but is expected to be active as a return man and reserve receiver. With all of that in mind, it is clear that Slayton could begin the 2026 season the same way he began the 2022 season — not getting a game-day jersey. Slayton said he sees himself as “just another playmaker” as a wide receiver. “I feel like we have a bunch in the room, a lot of really talented guys that we’ve added to the roster,” Slayton said. “I see myself as one of those guys.” Slayton has averaged 15.0 yards per catch throughout his career, and could still emerge as the “blow the top off the defense” vertical threat for Jaxson Dart. Slayton had double-sports hernia surgery during the offseason and missed all of the spring practices. He had a relatively quiet summer, with the exception of a four-catch, 58-yard performance in Week 2 of the preseason against the Miami Dolphins. Slayton admitted that he is still working his way back to full speed. “I feel like I had a solid summer. Obviously, trying to shake back from rehabbing and all of that. So, I had some bumps along the way. But overall, I think I put together a solid summer,” he said. “I feel pretty good. I wouldn’t say 100 yet, but definitely turning in the right direction.” Slayton has spent his career with the Giants defying expectations. It shouldn’t surprise anyone if he does it again.

title: 6 defensive linemen the NY Giants should consider signing
summary: The New York Giants general manager Joe Schoen addressed the media on Wednesday. He was asked about the roster and potential areas for improvement ahead of the Giants’ Week 1 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys. Schoen stated that the Giants are scouring available players and doing their due diligence, but then the topic of the […]
full_text: The New York Giants general manager Joe Schoen addressed the media on Wednesday. He was asked about the roster and potential areas for improvement ahead of the Giants’ Week 1 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys. Schoen stated that the Giants are scouring available players and doing their due diligence, but then the topic of the defensive line was addressed, and this was Schoen’s response: “We signed D.J. Reader, Shelby (Harris), we traded for C.J. Okoye, we’ve got DA (Darius Alexander). Bobby Jamison-Travis had a good camp. We’ve got a couple of vets on the practice squad, probably going to sign another one next week. So yeah, I feel good where we are right now. And again, we’ll continue, that’s something we’ll continue and see what opportunities are out there.“ Schoen mentioned that New York is interested in signing another veteran defensive tackle next week. The Giants had three defensive tackles and a big defensive end in for a workout on Wednesday: Benito Jones, David Blay, Aaron Graves, and Dawuane Smoot. Blay and Graves are both undrafted rookies this season, so they’re not veterans, but the Giants are certainly interested. Let’s explore Jones and Smoot, plus other available veteran defensive linemen that could help the Giants’ depth. Benito Jones Benito Jones is a 28-year-old 6-foot-1, 335-pound defensive lineman who went undrafted out of Mississippi in 2020. Jones started his career with Miami before playing two seasons in Detroit; he then returned to Miami for two seasons and spent the 2026 training camp on the Raiders’ practice squad. Jones only played 15 defensive snaps in preseason for the Las Vegas Raiders before being cut. Jones is a veteran with 59 pressures and four sacks to his name. He has 41 STOPs and has played 1,700 defensive snaps, with very poor PFF grades and a high missed-tackle rate. He has experience as a nose tackle and a 1-technique. Dawuane Smoot Smoot is much more of an edge defender than a defensive tackle, but he does align inside and has been used as a 4i-shade and a three-technique in certain situations. Smoot is entering his 10th season in the NFL, and all but one was spent in Jacksonville — he played 322 snaps for the Buffalo Bills in 2024 before returning to the Liam Coen-led Jaguars in 2025. Smoot has 203 pressures and 27 sacks throughout his career, while also earning 35 tackles for a loss and seven forced fumbles. He’s been a productive player with 3,725 defensive snaps to his name. He hasn’t had more than 20 pressures since 2022, but he did have a 50-pressure season in 2021. New York had him in for a workout this week, and he could give the Giants another physical edge with some inside pass-rushing ability, similar to Chauncey Golston. DaQuan Jones The 34-year-old played 424 snaps for the Buffalo Bills last season and recorded 13 STOPs and 21 pressures. He was an effective rotational player for Buffalo, and that would be his role with the Giants as well. Jones is long in the tooth but has not slowed down much from a productivity standpoint. He has 238 pressures and 25 sacks to his name. Adding Jones would give the Giants a geriatric defensive line room, but one filled with three reliable players that can allow Darius Alexander and Bobby Jameson-Travis to develop. Jihad Ward Is Jihad Ward coming back to New York? I have no clue, but the former Giant just had his best season with Dennard Wilson last year. The 32-year-old recorded an impressive 47 pressures and five sacks last season, operating as one of Wilson’s most effective twist-game players. Ward is more of a BIG defensive end, but he could be the veteran Schoen is referencing, for both Schoen and Wilson have experience with Jihad Ward. He is 6-5, 287 pounds, and has four consecutive seasons with more than 20 pressures, two of which were with the Giants. Elijah Garcia Hey, another familiar face! Garcia played well as a depth piece for the Giants in the final Brian Daboll years, but he was claimed by Atlanta late last season and spent this training camp in Christian Parker’s defense. Garcia did not make the final 53-man roster, but the 6-5, 302-pound former Giant could be a depth option. Eric Gregory Gregory is hardly a veteran, but I wanted to add him to the list. The 6-4, 320-pounder went undrafted in 2025 out of Arkansas and played 136 snaps for the Patriots last season. He earned two STOPS, three hurries, and had five tackles. Gregory recorded three consecutive seasons with 17 pressures in college, but was nearing Van Wilder status as a Razorback — he played six seasons of college football. He could be a depth piece for the Giants at a position of need.

title: How did NY Giants’ DT Darius Alexander really play this preseason?
summary: There is a lot of discussion surrounding the New York Giants as the regular season approaches. While much of the conversation has surrounded the offense, there are some storylines on the defense that demand our attention too. On the positive side, the Giants’ pass rush could be among the most formidable in the NFL (which […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 15: Darius Alexander #91 of the New York Giants tackles J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings during a preseason game at MetLife Stadium on August 15, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Mike Coppola/Getty Images) | Getty Images There is a lot of discussion surrounding the New York Giants as the regular season approaches. While much of the conversation has surrounded the offense, there are some storylines on the defense that demand our attention too. On the positive side, the Giants’ pass rush could be among the most formidable in the NFL (which remains a passing league), the linebacking corps looks deep and talented, and the Giants’ secondary could be primed to surprise skeptics. However, if there’s one area of concern it’s along the defensive line. In particular, 2025 third round pick Darius Alexander has been a frequent topic — and target — throughout the preseason. Giants’ great Carl Banks has said multiple times that the Giants need to see more from Alexander, while Pro Football Focus has pilloried him. But, did he play poorly? After all, the NFL is fast and the action along the defensive line can be messy to follow. Takes spawned in the moment can often prove to be somewhat less than accurate. So we’re going to go to the eye in the sky to get as accurate an assessment as we can. The bad Footing If there’s one issue that immediately stands out in Alexander’s game — and by “immediately” I mean on the very first play of the preseason — it’s that he can have bit of trouble staying on his feet. While I won’t go so far as to say that it’s a consistent problem, it does crop up multiple times. That said, there doesn’t seem to be a consistent issue with Alexander’s technique that leads to him being on the ground, and there seems to be several culprits. On the first play, a Vikings’ 18-yard prun, we see a good example of the issues that (should be) within Alexander’s ability to correct. We see Alexander lined up as the 5-technique on the outside shoulder of the Vikings’ left tackle. The Vikings execute a wide-zone run to that side, putting Alexander on the play-side. He starts off the play well, engaging the left tackle and bowing him back while giving up little ground. His hips are in the left B-gap, essentially closing the gap and helping to string the run laterally. That, however, is where things start to go wrong. As Alexander engages with the left tackle, his base begins to narrow and his pads rise. As that happens, the left guard gets piece of Alexander’s side, who isn’t able to absorb the block with a narrowed base while also moving laterally. That overbalances him, forces his pads up further, and allows the left tackle to put Alexander on the ground. From there, the guard is able to give Micah McFadden a shove, perhaps disrupting him enough that back is able to run through McFadden’s arms. Alexander generally does a very good job of playing half-man leverage and putting his hips in gaps to close them. However, he needs to do a better job of using his long arms to fend off blockers when he does so, as well as more consistently keeping a wide base to maintain his balance. This also showed up in a couple instances in Week 3 against the Jets. It seems to crop up most commonly when Alexander tries to run his feet and drive the blockers back, as opposed to keeping a wide base and simply eating the blocks. Notably, his hips rotate as he tries to drive the blocker, making it easier for the second linemen to move him laterally. There were also multiple instances of Alexander being tripped by his teammates as he either engaged blockers or penetrated into the backfield. It’s difficult to say whether that’s a “him” problem. For instance, we see Alexander against the Dolphins. Alexander is lined up in the right B-gap, between the right guard and right tackle. He engages the right guard with good leverage, also inserting his right arm into the A-gap to get a piece of the guard. Between squeezing the B-gap as well as putting his hips in the C-gap, Alexander is able to wall off the right side of the line and creates a path into the backfield for cornerback Nic Jones on a run blitz. That forces the back through the left A-gap. Alexander slows the right guard down well enough that Jack Kelly could insert himself into the left A-gap and blow up the play in the backfield. However, Kelly hesitates slightly which allows the back to work back to the right side. At the same time, Jones steps on Alexander’s leg, tripping him and allowing the right tackle to expand the gap and the back is able to pick up some dirty yards. Taken as a whole, we see that not only does Alexander need to continue to work on consistently playing with better technique, but also that his perceived level of play could improve when surrounded by starters. Anchor Alexander’s issues with consistency in his footing bleed into other areas of his game, and in particular his ability to consistently anchor against blockers. We got a good example early on against the Jets. Alexander is aligned as the 3-technique on the left guard’s outside shoulder. He makes an effort to stay low and play with a wide base off of the snap, which allows him to at least hold the guard. However Alexander fails to win inside leverage and gain control of the guard’s chest plate. Instead, the guard gains inside leverage on Alexander, using the grip on his chest plate to torque him laterally and prevent him from engaging with the center, who works up to the second level. This isn’t a huge loss for Alexander, particularly considering he’s able to occupy the guard well enough that that Micah McFadden is able to occupy the gap. The run itself, however, goes for a nice gain after Kelly attempts to occupy the same gap instead of flowing to the outside while Ar’Darius Washington is washed inside by a wide receiver who inserts into the box as a blocker. That said, this is a good example of how Alexander needs to become more consistent in his technique to fully take advantage of his athletic tools. The good Alexander’s tape is littered with flashes of impressive play, particularly as you begin to get a sense for what the Giants want to do on defense. Dennard Wilson’s scheme will likely depend heavily on living in nickel sets and attacking offenses with motion, the blitz, and the threat of the blitz. This isn’t the place to get into the weeds of how a defense can use stunts, twists, zone drops, simulated pressures, and blitzes to attack an offense — that’s for another piece. However, Alexander’s traits hold solid upside for helping to execute a modern defensive scheme. Athleticism Darius Alexander is a very good athlete, with a great first step and explosiveness. That showed up in flashes throughout the preseason. We’ll start with a play in run defense against the Vikings. Alexander begins the play lined up at 5-technique on the left tackle’s outside shoulder. The run is an outside zone to the right, putting Alexander on backside contain and pursuit. The Vikings attempt to account for him with a double-team from the tackle and tight end. However, Alexander is able to split the double team as the tackle releases to block at the second level. He runs the play down from behind as the back attempts to exploit a massive hole created when Josh Tupou gets washed out. This is the look just before Alexander closes on the play: There isn’t much between the back and the open field, and the run could have gone for another double-digit gain (if not much more). Instead, Alexander is able to discard the tight end’s block and close on the back quickly enough that this is only a 4-yard gain. Later in the game we get another good look at Alexander’s speed in space as he drops into a shallow coverage zone to create a path for Kelly on a zone blitz. Both Alexander and Chauncey Golston simulate a rush before dropping out in shallow coverage while linebackers Micah McFadden and Jack Kelly blitz, as well as…

Every Division’s ‘Wild Card’ for the 2026 NFL Season | Bleacher Report NFC East: New York Giants. The Ceiling: There’s a world in which Jaxson Dart takes off in his second season and becomes a star with top-notch support from an exciting skill-position group, a promising offensive line, a defense that features massive talent up front and an incoming head coach with Super Bowl pedigree. In that world, the Giants can shock the unpredictable NFC East. The Floor: Ultimately, it remains low with so many questionable variables. The sample is small for Dart, and two key cogs (Malik Nabers and Cam Skattebo) are coming back from major injuries. If the Eagles are the Eagles, a better defense helps Dallas bounce back, and Washington can rediscover what got it to the NFC title game in 2024, the Giants could be in for a third consecutive last-place campaign. The 2026 Giants Mission Statement "Our mission statement is to be the best team in the National Football League, and prove it." – John Harbaugh pic.twitter.com/74XGWOW875 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 2, 2026 NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites. | The Athletic 14. New York Giants. The voter highest on the Giants pointed to their defense. “They have a lot of pieces on defense, and I really liked their draft,” this exec said. “(John) Harbaugh will play everything close, and they’ll be in a ton of one-score games, and we’ll see what happens in the moment of truth. They’re a candidate for those games to play out really well.” Questions at quarterback, running back and receiver persist. “I like the Giants’ potential on defense,” another exec said. “Abdul Carter, Arvell Reese, Brian Burns. But then I don’t know how good that secondary is at corner. They lost Dexter Lawrence in the middle. On offense, Jaxson Dart’s health, Cam Skattebo’s health and Malik Nabers’ health are all concerns. There’s a lot of unknown.” Darius Slayton isn’t done proving himself to Giants after latest roster cut survival | New York Post Slayton, the longest-tenured Giant, has gotten used to uncertainty over his standing and the need to repeatedly prove his worth. “That’s mostly kind of been exacerbated by the turnover [in coaching staffs],” Slayton said. “Anytime there’s new people, there’s going to be that. Just for me, I’ve just been fortunate to be here for four staffs. I don’t take it personally. I understand that you have to show and prove yourself whenever there’s new [coaches]. That’s what I plan to do this year.” Giants’ Greg Newsome: ‘I like our chances’ against ‘dynamic’ Cowboys receivers | New York Daily News As the Steelers’ final play Hail Mary soared incomplete, Pickens dragged Newsome out of the back of the end zone by his helmet as the players engaged. Newsome fought Pickens off. And that set off a full-blown fight as the clock hit zero. Security guards appeared to pull Pickens off Newsome as their tussle spilled into one of the front rows of the stands. After the game, Newsome called Pickens a “fake tough guy” and said Pickens’ behavior was “unnecessary.” “He’s great at the catch point,” Newsome said of Pickens. “That’s something he’s been great at since he got in the league is just being able to make the tough catches. You’ve got number 88, CeeDee [Lamb], he can line up anywhere, do a lot of great things. Definitely great players but I like our chances.” 2026 NFL bold predictions: Potential surprises for 32 teams | ESPN.com Don’t be surprised if … tight end Isaiah Likely is a breakout star in New York. What I’m hearing: Giants coaches light up when talking about Likely, the free agent signee who came over from Baltimore with coach John Harbaugh.
