title: Super Bowl LXI odds: All 32 teams' odds to win the championship
summary: Every NFL team's win total, as well as odds to win their division, the conference and Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
It has been quite the NFL offseason for the Los Angeles Rams . First, they pulled off an absolute blockbuster of a trade in June by acquiring two-time and reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns . Los Angeles had already been the Super Bowl favorite, but the transaction pushed them from +800 to +650, then further to +600. Late August brought another gift, as  Aaron Donald  officially unretired to rejoin his former team. Now in September, the Rams sit at +500. That's well ahead of the second tier consisting of the Baltimore Ravens and Buffalo Bills at 10-1, as well as the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks at 12-1.

 

 The 2026 season will open with a Super Bowl rematch, with the Seahawks listed as 3.5-point favorites over the  New England Patriots . Caesars Sportsbook head of football Joey Feazel told ESPN, "With Seattle's recent win still fresh in bettors' minds, the public is likely to show strong interest in them again."

 Meanwhile, the Chargers were 11.5-point favorites over the Arizona Cardinals , the largest spread for a Week 1 game since 2012, according to ESPN Research, but that line has dropped to Chargers -10.5. Arizona is dead last on the Super Bowl odds board at 500-1 and is thus far an underdog in every one of its 2026 games.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings Sportsbook   and subject to change.

title: Who calls plays for every NFL team in 2026? What to know
summary: From veterans to newbies, here's everything you need to know about the NFL's playcallers in 2026.
full_text:
The 2026 season kicks off in six days with a rematch of Super Bowl LX, as the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots on Wednesday ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ).

 Josh McDaniels returns as the Patriots' playcaller. On the other side of the field, Brian Fleury replaces Seattle's 2025 offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak, who became the Las Vegas Raiders ' head coach this offseason, making him one of 18 new offensive playcallers this season.

 Veteran head coaches Andy Reid ( Kansas City Chiefs ), Kyle Shanahan ( San Francisco 49ers ) and Sean McVay ( Los Angeles Rams ) continue to make the calls in their creative offensive systems, but Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton surprisingly handed over playcalling duties to offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

 Meanwhile, some old faces have resurfaced in new places, including Mike McCarthy as Pittsburgh Steelers head coach, Frank Reich calling plays for the New York Jets , Brian Daboll as OC with the Tennessee Titans and Mike McDaniel as the Los Angeles Chargers ' OC.

 That doesn't even account for first-time playcallers, such as Baltimore Ravens OC Declan Doyle, Philadelphia Eagles OC Sean Mannion and Washington Commanders OC David Blough.

 With so many changes heading into 2026, here is a look at who is calling plays for all 32 teams, plus a key stat provided by ESPN Research.

 Jump to: 
 ARI  | ATL  | BAL  | BUF  | CAR  | CHI  |  CIN 
 CLE  | DAL  | DEN  | DET  | GB  | HOU  | IND 
 JAX  | KC  | LAC  | LAR | LV | MIA  | MIN 
 NE  | NO  | NYG  | NYJ  | PHI  | PIT  | SF 
 SEA  | TB  | TEN  | WSH 

 

 AFC EAST 
 

 

 Buffalo Bills 
 Playcaller:  Joe Brady, head coach

 Experience:  Brady has called plays for quarterback Josh Allen since mid-November 2023, going from interim offensive coordinator to offensive coordinator and now calling plays while taking over as head coach. He also called plays on the NFL level in his nearly two seasons with the Carolina Panthers .

 What to know:  While Brady has significant experience calling plays, he's a first-time head coach. He'll have the challenge of managing both jobs at once, while leading a team with high expectations. Success has been consistent with Brady calling plays for the Allen-led offense in Buffalo, as the Bills are second in points per game (29.6) and first in offensive EPA since 2024. A change, however, for the offense under Brady this season is that former tight ends coach Rob Boras is run game coordinator. -- Alaina Getzenberg 

 Key stat:  The Bills designed runs on 59% of their first-down plays since Brady took over offensive playcalling duties in November 2023 (highest percentage in NFL) after designing rushes on 42% of first downs in Allen's career before Brady took over (lowest percentage in NFL).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Miami Dolphins 
 Playcaller:  Bobby Slowik, offensive coordinator

 Experience: This is Slowik's second season with the Dolphins after spending 2025 as the team's passing game coordinator. He previously spent two seasons as the Houston Texans ' offensive coordinator.

 What to know:  The Dolphins' poor passing game in 2025 could be attributed to a decline in quarterback play, an injury to WR  Tyreek Hill and lack of legitimate options once Hill went down. Slowik's first season in Houston coincided with QB  C.J. Stroud 's rookie season, when Stroud was named AP Rookie of the Year and the Texans finished seventh in passing yards. The production tapered off the following season and the Texans finished 22nd in total yards. Slowik will tailor this Dolphins offense around running back De'Von Achane and quarterback Malik Willis -- who offers a more dynamic skill set than any quarterback he has ever worked with. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques 

 Key stat:  The Dolphins recorded the NFL's second-highest screen attempt percentage (14%) last season with Slowik as senior passing game coordinator.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 New England Patriots 
 Playcaller: Josh McDaniels, offensive coordinator

 Experience: In his 25th NFL season and 20th with the Patriots, McDaniels enters his 15th year as the team's offensive coordinator (three different stints). McDaniels turned 50 on April 22.

 What to know:  One of the themes of training camp has been QB Drake Maye taking more ownership of the offense because it's his second year in McDaniels' system. McDaniels leads an experienced offensive staff that includes former NFL head coaches and/or coordinators in Doug Marrone (offensive line), Thomas Brown (tight ends/passing game coordinator) and Todd Downing (wide receivers). -- Mike Reiss 

 Key stat:  The Patriots had the second-highest average pass distance in the NFL last season (8.7), the highest rate for a McDaniels-led offense since 2017 (8.8 with Patriots).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 New York Jets 
 Playcaller:  Frank Reich, offensive coordinator

 Experience:  It's his first season with the Jets, but Reich is a seasoned playcaller -- having handled the responsibility for the Chargers, Colts and Panthers.

 What to know:  It'll be interesting to see if Reich, 64, back in the league after a two-year hiatus, has added any wrinkles to his system. His last two seasons (2023-24 in Carolina) weren't good. His biggest challenge is helping quarterback Geno Smith reduce his interceptions. He will lean into the running game and will use more 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 WR, 2 TE) than usual. The Jets finished 29th in scoring, their 10th straight season in the bottom third. Things can only go up, right? -- Rich Cimini 

 Key stat:  The Colts had five receivers in pass routes on 75% of their plays in Reich's tenure as head coach (2018-22), the second-highest percentage in the NFL in that span behind only the Chiefs (77%), per NFL Next Gen Stats.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 AFC NORTH 

 

 

 Baltimore Ravens 
 Playcaller:  Declan Doyle, offensive coordinator

 Experience:  Doyle is calling plays for the first time of his eight-year NFL career. He was the offensive coordinator last season for the Chicago Bears , but head coach Ben Johnson called the plays. Doyle was previously the tight ends coach with the Denver Broncos (2023-24) and an offensive assistant with the New Orleans Saints (2019-22).

 

 What to know:  Doyle, who turned 30 in March, is the youngest playcaller in the league. The players have praised Doyle's system for its details. Quarterback Lamar Jackson said Doyle has been "like a wizard." Wide receiver Zay Flowers has called him "a genius." One of the biggest changes has been putting Jackson under center after he lined up in the pistol for 95% of his NFL career. Doyle has been tough on the two-time NFL Most Valuable Player, from his footwork to his reads. "He's grading me like I'm a rookie or something," Jackson said. "He's always on me. But I appreciate it." -- Jamison Hensley 

 Key stat:  With Doyle as offensive coordinator, Bears QB Caleb Williams had the second-most pass attempts outside the pocket last season (128), trailing Bo Nix (133).  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Cincinnati Bengals 
 Playcaller:  Zac Taylor, head coach

 Experience: Taylor is entering his eighth year as the Bengals' head coach. He has been the playcaller for all eight seasons.

 What to know:  Taylor's playcalling has come under fire over the years. But whether it was Brian Callahan or Dan Pitcher serving as offensive coordinator, Taylor has held onto the reins. This season, Taylor is looking for new ways to create a more explosive offense, especially with Joe Burrow back under center. Even with Burrow out for nine games last season, Cincinnati finished 13th in points per drive. But the big plays have been lacking, which is a focal point for a unit that features Burrow, wide receivers Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins and running back Chase Brown . -- Ben Baby 

 Key stat:  Over the past four seasons, the Bengals have the highest designed pass percentage in the NFL (67%).  -- ESPN Research

title: NFL players, coaches, GMs under the most pressure in 2026
summary: Can Baker Mayfield and C.J. Stroud play their way to big contracts? Is Aaron Glenn on thin ice with the Jets? Which 2024 first-rounders have fifth-year options at stake?
full_text:
Editor's note: Arizona receiver Michael Wilson was originally on this list, but he signed a new extension on Thursday. 

 Some people around the NFL have more riding on the 2026 season than others. The vast majority of players are on one-year deals or have limited or no guaranteed money waiting for them in 2027. Every coordinator and assistant coach is one bad year away from potentially looking for work. And although a fair number of head coaches and general managers have real job security, others might have a storied career with one team come down to a missed field goal or a contested catch at the wrong time -- to which John Harbaugh and Sean McDermott can attest.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Today, I'm looking at the players, coaches and executives who might be most impacted by what they do -- or don't do -- during the 2026 campaign. Perhaps it is a player in position to make life-changing money if he has a good season at the right time. Perhaps it is someone on the verge of losing their path to a starting role. It could also mean coaches and executives looking to lock up another contract with a successful year.

 Even within this group, though, there are a few players who could really see their future diverge into one of two dramatically different paths solely based on what they do over the next 17 games. Let's open things up there. Here are 22 people around the NFL with the most to gain or lose in 2026.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Stroud | Pickens | Mayfield | Murray 
 Three coordinators | Porter | Jones 
 Colts brass | Hunter | Glenn 
 Fifth-year options | Hall of Fame candidates 

 
 

 

 C.J. Stroud , QB, Houston Texans 
 I'll start with the player who might have a wider range of outcomes heading into the season than anyone. There aren't many candidates in any given year who have a shot at coming out of the campaign as the highest-paid player in NFL history. But Stroud has the potential to be that player if things go right. There's also a world where things go south and he's competing for his job -- or on another roster altogether -- in 2027.

 In a what-have-you-done-for-me-lately sports universe, Stroud's disastrous postseason has dominated offseason discussion around the fourth-year pro. Turning the ball over seven times (and being lucky to avoid more) in two games will do that. Texans fans will look at what the Seahawks did on the other side of the bracket, with a dominant defense and a quarterback who avoided turning the ball over at all in three games, and rue what happened in January. Between teams such as the Chiefs and Ravens missing the playoffs altogether, and the Broncos showing up in the AFC Championship Game without their starting quarterback, the 2025 season might go down as a missed opportunity for the Texans.

 

 The Texans should feel like Super Bowl contenders again in 2026, given that they return virtually everyone of note on an elite defense, but there's unquestionable anxiety about Stroud. Perhaps that's unwarranted. Stroud posted a 61.7 QBR during the 2025 regular season, which was good for 11th in the league, ahead of quarterbacks such as  Trevor Lawrence and Bo Nix . He did that with inconsistent offensive line play and a moribund run game, issues that have plagued Houston throughout Stroud's first three seasons in the NFL.

 My concern is that those issues haven't really been resolved. General manager Nick Caserio has churned through running back and offensive line changes yet again this offseason, but there are still legitimate questions about the sort of help Stroud will receive. Veterans Braden Smith and Wyatt Teller haven't been able to carve out starting roles, and Smith could miss a few weeks with a plantar fascia injury . New lead back David Montgomery  is moving from one of the most run-friendly offenses in the league to one of its least in terms of expected yards per carry. And wideout Jayden Higgins is already out for the year after tearing an ACL , leading the Texans to trade for Kayshon Boutte , who will have to learn the offense on the fly.

 That might be the most realistic shift between the Stroud some saw as a rookie and the one who hasn't significantly built on that impressive debut campaign. He needs help. Stroud might not be able to single-handedly propel the offense forward in the way that the league's true high-end quarterbacks can. That rookie year was built on an unsustainable interception rate (1.0%) and an impressive penchant for picking up chunks of yardage (8.2 yards per attempt). Stroud hasn't been close to either number since then.

 The 2024-25 version of Stroud is still a very solid starter, and I'd argue he hasn't gotten much support, but that's a different player with a different ceiling from the one who immediately propelled the Texans into contention in 2023. There's nothing wrong with this version of Stroud, and if the Texans haven't resolved the infrastructure issues surrounding him this offseason, it's where Stroud is likely to settle by the end of the 2026 season. But if the run game finally gets going, I still believe Stroud has another level, and a season like his 2023 campaign might be enough to earn the young QB the biggest contract in NFL history.

 If the postseason issues linger into the 2027 season and the Texans disappoint, would the Texans be willing to consider what life looks like without Stroud on what could be a franchise-limiting second contract? The difference between those two scenarios might be $100 million or more in guaranteed money.

 

 
 

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys 
 Prove it. That was the mantra for Pickens heading into the 2025 season, after the Steelers clearly decided that they didn't want to move forward with their mercurial wideout on a significant contract extension. Pittsburgh dealt Pickens to the Cowboys for a third-round pick, and with a major upgrade at quarterback, he produced a career season. Pickens set career highs in receptions (93), receiving yards (1,429) and touchdowns (nine), earning his first trip to the Pro Bowl.

 Prove it again. The Cowboys also weren't willing to sign Pickens to a long-term contract after the season, instead using the franchise tag to retain his services on a one-year, $27.3 million pact. Were the Cowboys concerned about their ability to keep Pickens motivated? Were they unwilling to commit significant money to a second receiver given what they're already paying Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb ? Or did they just not believe that Pickens' 2025 season represented what he'll do moving forward?

 

 Some combination of the three might be true, but if Pickens can produce a repeat season, it won't matter. The Cowboys spent heavily to fix their defense this offseason, and they might not be interested in a second franchise tag for Pickens in 2027, which would cost more than $32 million. Hitting unrestricted free agency as a 26-year-old wide receiver could be a massive opportunity for Pickens, who would potentially be the best player available.

 

 
 

 Baker Mayfield , QB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 The " Baker Mayfield Rule " holds that the veteran quarterback's performance is inversely correlated with how much confidence the public has in his ability. More doubt, more success. As soon as Mayfield started earning consideration as an MVP candidate around the midway point of the 2025 season, his performance cratered, taking Tampa Bay's season along for the ride.

 Are the Bucs testing this corollary by refusing to come to terms with the pending 2027 unrestricted free agent on a contract extension? He unquestionably exceeded the initial expectations on him when he joined Tampa Bay to compete with Kyle Trask for the starting job. Mayfield hasn't missed a start in three years, he won a playoff game over the Eagles in 2023, and he ranks 14th in QBR over his run with the Bucs, between quarterbacks such as  Jared Goff (12th) and Trevor Lawrence (16th). Goff makes $53 million per year, while Lawrence is at $55…

title: How Panthers QB Bryce Young, playcaller Brad Idzik will mesh in 2026
summary: Carolina believes a more aggressive approach under first-time playcaller Brad Idzik can help franchise QB Bryce Young reach another level.
full_text:
THE CAROLINA PANTHERS ' starting offense slumped to start the 2026 NFL preseason. Fourth-year quarterback Bryce Young and offensive coordinator Brad Idzik hadn't found their footing. The offense managed 26 total yards in its first four drives together.

 But on the fifth drive, against the Jacksonville Jaguars' backup defense in the second week of the preseason at EverBank Stadium, Idzik, Young and the Panthers adjusted for a seven-play, 58-yard touchdown drive. Young moved around the pocket and made quick tosses down the field to tight end Tommy Tremble and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan , and the offense as a whole functioned with urgency during the series.

 It was a glimmer. It was a glimpse of how this offense can operate with Young and Idzik leading a new, more aggressive charge heading into the 2026 regular season that begins with the Panthers hosting the Chicago Bears on Sept. 13 ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 Idzik is new to playcalling, but he's not new to Young. The coordinator, now in his third year with the title, will take control of those playcalling duties after inheriting the job from coach Dave Canales this offseason. And with a new voice in the quarterback's helmet on game days, the hope is that Young -- with a lucrative contract extension at stake -- will flourish during the biggest season of his NFL career and the Panthers will make another postseason run.

 "He's definitely been aggressive, which is huge for us," Young said about Idzik and his ability to guide the QB and the game. "That's a part of the offense we can build upon and we can expand in. We have the guys -- I have all the faith in the world in our guys out there. So giving them opportunities down the field; try to be more explosive, more dynamic."

 
 THE YOUNG-LED CAROLINA offense failed to get off to fast starts over the past two seasons with Canales calling plays.

 The Panthers' offense ranked 21st and 26th in first-quarter scoring average in each of the past two seasons, respectively. While Carolina had the 15th-ranked first-quarter time of possession average in 2024, that status dropped to 29th in 2025.

 

 The team has won five total games in the first eight weeks of the past two seasons during the Canales era, partially because the offense hasn't gotten off to hot starts on Sundays, especially before the calendar flips to November.

 But after finishing 30th in passing yardage and 29th in total yardage in 2024, and 26th and 27th in those respective categories in 2025, Carolina wants to push the tempo with Idzik at the controls.

 In theory, a quick and efficient procedure should allow the Panthers to control the momentum when Young is directing traffic on the field.

 "The biggest thing, and I think this would come in Year 3 -- whether I was calling it or Dave was -- is the aggressive nature of the pre-snap, breaking the huddle, getting to the line, and having confidence in if we're not checking a play, let's get this thing rolling," Idzik said. "Let's roll off the ball and put the defense on their heels."

 Training camp was the time to test the tandem's focus on urgency. And while the summer might have been a fun return to football for Idzik, Young and the Carolina offense, it wasn't necessarily smooth.

 Young had practices in which he looked like a bona fide star against his own defense. He also was stifled for prolonged stretches of joint practices against the Jaguars and Houston Texans .

 The starting offense's preseason performance will also do little to squash the outside concern for slow starts. Idzik and Young, though, feel comfortable with each other enough to make adjustments in the games that actually count.

 "I think it's been a really good learning period for us," Young said about training camp following the joint practice against the Jaguars.

 Backup quarterback Kenny Pickett , who signed with the team in March, has been in the room with Young and Idzik all summer. So has third-year quarterbacks coach Will Harriger. Both have seen Young and Idzik sort through the intricacies of each other's work.

 The comfort is there, and onlookers say it's evident.

 "I just think it's the natural evolution of an ever-deepening relationship," Herriger said. "And it's just nice that now, as the playcaller, [Idzik] has already got those two years of kind of developing a feel and kind of a general idea of what he thinks Bryce is going to say, but then ... he obviously makes a great attempt to get his opinion on that stuff as it goes."

 "You can tell it's [Young's] third year in the system," Pickett said. "I feel like he has a really good grasp of the offense. ... Has had these plays multiple times versus multiple different looks, so he knows where to go with the football with what he sees. He's playing really fast, so it's been really cool to work with him."

 

 
 THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Idzik and Young has naturally evolved over the past three offseasons. But the 34-year-old coordinator has gone out of his way to build a bond with the signal-caller, too.

 Since his arrival in 2024, the coordinator and his wife, Emily, have hosted the quarterbacks at their home during offseason downtime.

 To Idzik, whose father, John Jr., was an NFL general manager, and grandfather, John Sr., was an NFL offensive coordinator, the ability to relate to his players on and off the field -- in particular, his quarterback -- is paramount.

 "Anytime you can welcome someone into your life and into your personal space, I think it's an important invitation of your intentions," Idzik said. "And him understanding I don't want to just go grab dinner at the fancy restaurant. I want you to come over to my house, so you understand who I am and what I care about. I want you to meet my wife and my dogs and see my living space so you have an idea of ... why I coach. This is my 'why.'"

 The message has been received by Young, who inherits his fourth playcaller in as many NFL seasons.

 "Just being able to meet the people in our lives, have that relationship [off the field], you want to go that much harder, do that much more for those people when you know the other side," Young said.

 That personal connection has bled into their shared work on 200 South Tryon Street. Young has trust in Idzik, and the coordinator wants the quarterback's continuous input, no matter how much it clashes with his point of view.

 

 It's a partnership, and Young and Idzik's careers will be intertwined based on how the offense performs this season. Finding a common ground is essential, not only for the two main stewards of the offense, but the unit and the team as well.

 "As a quarterback, you gotta get comfortable with the words yourself and where all the bones are buried on plays," Idzik said. "And then from there, he does a great job of recommending things that fit what we're trying to do as a whole."

 "We've been doing so much work behind the scenes," Young said. "So since Day 1, since right when he got hired and first gave me a call from that first conversation till now, it's been great being able to work with him. I feel like we have great chemistry and a great working relationship, so I'm excited for it to continue to grow."

 Canales, during his first season at the helm for the franchise, benched Young three weeks into the 2024 regular season.

 The then-second-year QB stood on the sideline with a clipboard for five games, as well-traveled veteran fill-in Andy Dalton led the Panthers to a 1-4 record. Young reemerged as the starter in Week 8 after his replacement sustained a thumb injury in a minor car accident.

 Canales has noted publicly that Young showed improved command of the offense during his first game back in the starting lineup against the Denver Broncos in a 28-14 road loss. Young has since thrown for 4,891 yards, 36 touchdowns and 15 interceptions, while leading the Panthers to a 2025 NFC South title -- albeit with an 8-9 overall record (Dalton started one loss due to injury) -- in his last…

title: Cowboys first-rounder Caleb Downs living up to the hype
summary: Downs has exceeded expectations throughout the offseason as the safety heads toward his NFL debut against the Giants in Week 1.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- When the rookies put on their training camp skit in the Dallas Cowboys ' final days in Oxnard, California, there was little doubt what role Caleb Downs would play.

 From the time the Cowboys selected him in the first round to the final camp practice last week at The Star, Downs and defensive coordinator Christian Parker have been within arm's length of each other.

 Parker walking him through different situations, teaching him different techniques before practice and during breaks. Downs listening and learning through it all.

 So when Downs appeared for the skit in a Parker-like sweatsuit, a pair of Jordans and stylish glasses, then spoke about Jay-Z, everybody in the room knew who he was. Downs would only smirk, "It was cool."

 Brian Schottenheimer liked it, too.

 "The mannerisms were very good," the coach said. "Christian's one of those guys that he is wanting to be in games and wanting to be doing extra, and they spend a lot of time together. You can see them before practice, working together. I think that's important for any player, but certainly a young guy that has the high expectations of himself that Caleb does."

 

 Downs will make his NFL debut in nine days when the Cowboys take on the New York Giants . It's a moment he knew would be coming for years, well before he starred at Alabama for one season, becoming the first true freshman to lead the Crimson Tide in tackles, and at Ohio State, where he was a two-time All-American and a winner of the Jim Thorpe Award as the country's best defensive back.

 Since the Cowboys selected Downs at No. 11, trading up one spot with the Miami Dolphins to make sure they would get their priority player, Downs has done nothing but show he is ready.

 "He's very willing," Parker said. "He's very curious."

 The curiosity is the product of growing up with a father, Gary Downs , who had a six-year career as a running back with three teams, and a family steeped in the game. He mastered three different defenses in three years in college.

 

 When Downs arrived in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, in the winter of 2023, he prepared so much early on that the coaches had to make sure he knew he could not play in the Tide's bowl game. At Ohio State, it took him weeks to learn Jim Knowles' scheme, and then last year under Matt Patricia, who brought a complex scheme developed under Bill Belichick with the New England Patriots, Downs picked up in weeks not only the responsibilities of his own position but what everybody else was supposed to do too.

 "He's hungry for knowledge," secondary coach Ryan Smith said. "He wants to learn. He wants immediate feedback, whether it's in the meeting room or walking through or just working on his footwork. ... He's definitely urgent, and I appreciate that about him. That's what you get usually with guys who've been in the league for a while. For him coming in as a rookie, it's cool to see."

 He is being asked to play the nickel spot in the defense but also working as a deep safety at times. In the nickel, he has been asked to cover receivers such as  CeeDee Lamb and KaVontae Turpin . In the joint practices against the Los Angeles Rams and New Orleans Saints , he defended Puka Nacua and Chris Olave .

 "Mike Tyson said success breeds confidence and confidence breeds success," Downs said. "So I feel like those two work together and when you win at things and you do good at things, it allows you to feel more confident. And then when you succeed, it just continues to grow from there."

 

 Tyson also said everybody has a plan until they get hit. As a slot defender, Downs also carries serious run game responsibilities, and he has been tasked in practice with taking on lead blocks from guard Tyler Smith and tackle Tyler Guyton .

 "That's one of the things when you run some of those things that we have where he's got to fit the gaps every once in a while, you're going to run into an unfavorable matchup," Schottenheimer said. "But it's no different than if you're a safety or a corner and a big back like [Baltimore's]  Derrick Henry gets out in space. It's like, 'OK, this might hurt a little bit, but I got to get him down.'"

 Defensive passing game coordinator Derrick Ansley used a modern-game description of Downs.

 "What he is, he's a positionless player," Ansley said. "He can play most anything if you get a chance to teach it to him. He can learn it on the fly."

 Coaches say he rarely makes the same mistake twice. He can recognize patterns and concepts quickly, yet as camp went on, he was one of the last defensive backs to record an interception.

 His first came in his a camp practice in front of Cowboys fans at Ford Center at The Star on Aug. 25.

 Guarding Ryan Flournoy in tight red zone work, Downs was able to close the space and come down with the Dak Prescott pass in the back of the end zone. In an instant, he turned and punted the ball -- like other defenders had done in Oxnard -- in celebration.

 To Schottenheimer, it wasn't done to mark that he finally had a takeaway.

 "He knows there's a lot more to come, but he and Dak were having some good trash talk back and forth, which is good," Schottenheimer said. "And it was actually a little smirk on Dak's face when he saw it was Caleb that got the interception. I think he was excited -- not excited he threw an interception -- but that we're seeing the growth of what's going to be a really, really great player."

title: Cowboys' Luepke trades jersey number to Von Miller for chicken ownership stake
summary: Miller was able to take over No. 40 from the fullback after a brief and interesting negotiation following the future Hall of Fame pass rusher's arrival to the Cowboys.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- What do you get when a poultry science major from Texas A&M and someone with a finance degree from North Dakota State become teammates on the Dallas Cowboys ? A number switch. 
 
Linebacker Von Miller obtained No. 40 from fullback Hunter Luepke after a brief and interesting negotiation following the future Hall of Fame pass rusher's arrival to the Cowboys. 
 
Luepke earned a small ownership stake in Greener Pastures Chicken, of which Miller is a co-owner, after passing on, among other things, "chicken for life." 
 
He is now wearing No. 30.

 "I would have to say it's got to be the first in National Football League history that a jersey swap has been done with ownership of a chicken farm," Miller said. "He's learned from the best with the negotiators here with the Cowboys."

 Other notable co-owners of Greener Pastures Chicken? Current and former quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes , Drew Brees and Nick Foles . 
 
"It's the chicken of champions, so it was only right for Hunter to be a part of that too," Miller said. "He won three national championships in college. So it was a great fit for us. It was a great fit for him, and I'm happy that we were able to get it done." 
 
Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said he would not get involved in the number switch after Miller signed. 
 
Since the NFL allowed single-digit numbers to be worn by everyone other than offensive or defensive linemen, Schottenheimer said things have become trickier. He also relayed a story from last year about a player who thought his jersey number was going to be taken from him after a veteran's arrival. 
 
In Schottenheimer's coaching past, he has seen players trade numbers for cars and Rolex watches. 
 
"If a guy wants a jersey bad enough and he's been around the league a while, he usually has enough capital, cash to get things done," Schottenheimer said. "And I think these guys found a way to get this thing resolved."

title: Expectations for Jaguars' Liam Coen, Trevor Lawrence in 2026
summary: The Jaguars haven't made back-to-back postseason appearances this century. But they think 2026 can be different with Coen and Lawrence.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- In the days after the Jacksonville Jaguars ' 27-24  playoff loss to the Buffalo Bills in January, team owner Shad Khan huddled with head coach Liam Coen, general manager James Gladstone and executive vice president of football operations Tony Boselli.

 Khan was delighted with what the trio accomplished in its first year: a 13-4 record and the AFC South title. But he wanted to know how the Jaguars would avoid a repeat of what happened the past two times his franchise came out of nowhere, won the AFC South and made the playoffs.

 "The No. 1 thing is we don't regress," Khan said in late March. "We all remember the prior seasons. You have great success [in 2017 and 2022] and then ... So really, literally after the last home game, all of us were really focused on, OK, once you get over the bitterness of the loss, what are we going to do here that we don't regress?"

 In 2018, the Jaguars went 5-11 because of injuries, quarterback Blake Bortles ' struggles and a fractured locker room . In 2023, they had a winning record (9-8) but injuries to key offensive players (such as receivers Zay Jones and Christian Kirk ) led to a 1-5 finish that Khan called an " organizational failure ." Both finishes cost the franchise back-to-back playoff appearances for the first time since 1998-99. There are only three teams in the NFL without back-to-back playoff berths since 1999 -- the Cleveland Browns , Washington Commanders and Jaguars.

 

 Why, Khan asked, will that not be the case in 2026?

 After a relatively quiet offseason -- with just one signing in free agency (running back Chris Rodriguez Jr .) and no first-round pick because of last year's Travis Hunter trade -- the Jaguars believe the answers are already in the building. A rock-solid culture  is being built by Coen, and Trevor Lawrence  is ascending into the top tier of NFL quarterbacks after a promising end to the 2025 season and productive offseason .

 "I feel really good," Lawrence said in June. "I feel really healthy. ... I think I'm throwing it as good as ever. I think the chemistry with the guys is really, really good."

 If they're correct, the Jaguars will be in the playoffs again come January, marking the first time they would have accomplished back-to-back berths this century. The quest starts Sunday, Sept. 13 against the Browns ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "Our mindset is we've got to go prove it and go earn it because consistency is the truest measure of performance at the end of the day," Coen said on the first day of training camp. "And there's a lot of guys in this locker room that, when I took this job, have said ... 'How do we become a consistent, respected organization?' That's what this is all about."

 
 Building on Coen's culture  
 When Coen, Gladstone and Boselli took over the team in 2025, the first thing they tackled was the team culture .

 In 2024, the Jaguars went 3-10 in one-score games (the most such losses in a single season in the Super Bowl era), finished 31st in total defense, forced the fewest turnovers in the league (nine) and was outscored by 115 points. Khan fired coach Doug Pederson after that season and GM Trent Baalke weeks later . 

 In the days after being hired as the next head coach, Coen laid out his master plan for success: play fast and aggressively, be fundamentally sound, be good at situational football, and be mentally and physically tough.

 

 To do that the Jaguars needed a roster full of players who understood that standard -- they drafted a " unicorn " in Hunter after trading up to No. 2 overall and added players familiar with Coen like center  Robert Hainsey . There was also a focus on synergy and alignment between Coen, Gladstone and Boselli, something that was not present under the previous regime of Pederson and Baalke.

 It was evident early in the season that things had changed. In Week 3, the Jaguars beat the Houston Texans 17-10 with a late touchdown and game-saving interception. Then in the following week, the Jaguars outrushed the San Francisco 49ers by nearly double (151 to 83) in a 26-21 victory. And the week after that, they beat Kansas City Chiefs  31-28 on "Monday Night Football," getting a 99-yard interception return for a touchdown by Devin Lloyd and a game-winning touchdown run from Lawrence with 23 seconds remaining.

 Things stalled a little bit with back-to-back losses to the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams , as well as a blown 19-point fourth-quarter lead at Houston in Week 10. But the Jaguars finished the season with eight consecutive victories, clinching their third AFC South title in franchise history.

 The winning culture the front office wanted was established. But in 2026, the quick success of last season doesn't matter.

 "We haven't done anything to rest on our laurels here," Coen said. "We're not in a place to hang out and just kind of chill, right? Everything we're doing is trying to attack an edge. Last year was about finding an edge and creating an edge. And now we are attacking these edges with a relentless pursuit."

 Players have embraced Coen's approach of starting over.

 "We've talked about it as players, just that we have the opportunity to continue to get better," said Hainsey, who joined the Jaguars last year after playing under Coen with the Buccaneers. "But like I said, it doesn't just happen. It happens because we do the right things now and throughout training camp and during the weeks throughout the season and all those things."

 

 Defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton was a rookie in 2020 when the Jaguars went 1-15. He was part of the 2022 division title team and the falloff in 2023 and 2024. But he says what the Jaguars did last season feels much more sustainable.

 "We all buy into [the culture reset]," he said. "... I think you could buy into a culture and still not be successful, but we're not really worried about necessarily the results right now. Just trying to home in on our technique and what we need to do, where we need to be at. And then that's going to lead us to our results."

 
 Is Lawrence unlocked? 
 The 2021 No. 1 overall pick has been an enigma in Jacksonville since being drafted.

 There was a dysfunctional rookie season with head coach Urban Meyer, then multiple injuries (toe, ankle, shoulder, knee, concussion) and sporadic spurts of elite play under Pederson from 2022-24. Even the first nine games of the 2025 season under Coen were puzzling: a 41.4 Total QBR, 222 passing yards per game, 10 touchdowns, seven interceptions, 172 rushing yards and four rushing touchdowns. The Jaguars went 5-4.

 After that? He was one of the NFL's best quarterbacks with a league-best 24 total touchdowns, 77 QBR (third), 251 passing yards per game and only five turnovers in the last eight games of 2025. The Jaguars went 8-0.

 Lawrence's resurgence was sparked by Coen's " let it rip" direction in a meeting after the Week 10 Texans loss. But the feeling inside the franchise is that he will let it rip again in 2026, based on how Lawrence has improved this summer.

 "If I had to pick one or two [words to describe Lawrence's offseason], progress would probably be in there," offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said. "[Also with] process, consistency. The consistency to show up day after day after day and build on what we had last year, but not take any of those details and fundamentals and foundational steps for granted and continue to work over and over ... whether it's a drop and technique and fundamentals or whether it's a read or whether it's just calling a certain play or a certain motion, all of those things are so important."

 

 For Lawrence, this offseason was about gaining a graduate-level understanding of Coen's offense, not rehabbing from an injury or changing his footwork the way he did last year. Nor was it adjusting to a new playcaller, as he did in 2023.

 Lawrence is more confident in his progressions, adjustments, when to kill a play and what to call instead. His mind, he…

title: Chiefs rush to rebuild defense around veteran Chris Jones
summary: Kansas City is betting that highly drafted rookies Peter Woods and R Mason Thomas will give its future hall of famer the support he's been missing.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- This summer for Chris Jones was different.

 The realization really hit Jones, the Chiefs' star pass rusher, in early June, when he kept looking around in the huddle. He was reminded again in early August, during one of the Chiefs' first fully-padded practices. A large number of the reps taken featured Jones lined up next to rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods , the Chiefs' second of two first-round picks. On the other side of Jones, the defensive end sometimes was R Mason Thomas , another rookie, this one the Chiefs selected in the draft's second round.

 Of course, Jones is aware that Woods, 21, and Thomas, 22, are a decade younger than him. And of course, one of the teammates Woods and Thomas have gravitated to the most ahead of the upcoming season is Jones, who at age 32 is the Chiefs' best defender -- and their longest-tenured, too.

 

 "That's a nice way to say you're old," Jones said, laughing. "I've been in the league going on 11 years, so, I mean, if they paid attention to the Chiefs any bit, then they've probably seen me on the field."

 Youth is just one element of the Chiefs' changes on defense. Even Jones' fellow starting interior lineman is Khyiris Tonga , who joined the team in free agency. All those major changes surrounding Jones -- who has always been the sun around which the Chiefs defense has revolved during their dynastic run -- were what the Chiefs believe this offseason was necessary for the franchise to return to contention after missing the playoffs for the first time since 2014.

 No other part of the roster received as many newcomers, draft capital and overhaul from the previous year than along the Chiefs' defensive line. In fact, Woods and Thomas are the first duo of defensive linemen the Chiefs selected in the first and second rounds of the same draft since 2002 (defensive tackle Ryan Sims and defensive end Eddie Freeman). All those efforts, led by coach Andy Reid, general manager Brett Veach and longtime coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, were made to fix one of the team's biggest issues: the pass rush.

 

 "Besides Chris, you want guys that can [get] pressure," Reid said. "If you leave these quarterbacks [time] in this league, and let them sit there [in the pocket], they're going to rip you apart. You've got to make them uncomfortable -- and you have to have the guys to be able to do that.

 "The guys Brett bought in have that ability. It's just a matter of getting it done."

 Unlike any previous year under Spagnuolo, who joined the Chiefs in 2019, this year's path for the defense to be its most effective is expected to be made through the improved production of the linemen.

 In early August, one particular rep was a glimpse of what the Chiefs hope to see plenty in the future. With the offense in a passing situation, quarterback Patrick Mahomes received the snap from the shotgun. One side of the Chiefs' pass rush was Jones and defensive end George Karlaftis , the four-year veteran and team's most experienced and accomplished edge rusher. Woods and Thomas worked from the left side. Together, the four players -- and an overload blitz with two extra defenders -- were able to pressure Mahomes, forcing the quarterback to throw a short pass in less than two seconds. The result of the play was an interception by nickel cornerback Chris Roland-Wallace .

 The following week, during camp's hardest stretch, something occurred that rarely happened last season: Jones was on the sideline -- and the defense was still able to beat the offensive line's protection. In a matchup against left tackle Josh Simmons , Woods was able to leap in the air and use his right hand to knock down Mahomes' pass without touching the quarterback. When the play was over, the second-closest defender next to Mahomes was Thomas.

 "We got some dawgs in the room," Jones said. "Peter Woods, I love that guy. He's a young bull. R Mason is going to contribute a lot for us in the pass rush."

 Later this month, the Chiefs will open their season on "Monday Night Football" against the Denver Broncos . Much of the Chiefs' 2026 campaign -- after finishing last season with an underwhelming 6-11 record -- will be determined by the play of Mahomes, who is on track to be the team's starter for Week 1 after recovering from the torn ACL and LCL in his left knee.

 For Jones, he was blunt when he shared how he will measure the defense's overall performance, the one statistic he believes has to change the most.

 "We've got to get more sacks," Jones said after the Chiefs had just 35, the fifth fewest in the league, last season, including just 21.5 recorded by the D-line. "It affected the defense tremendously. If we want this defense to be a success, we've got to get more sacks."

 

 ALMOST A YEAR ago, the troubling signs for the Chiefs' pass rush were evident as early as their first game.

 In São Paulo, the Chiefs barely touched Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert  when they didn't blitz (their two sacks were a byproduct of sending extra defenders). Frustrated by being double-teamed for most of the game -- and the lack of pressure from his fellow teammates -- Jones switched positions and lined up on the edge to get a one-on-one matchup for the Chargers' pivotal third-and-14 snap. With the Chargers leading by six points, Spagnuolo's unit was one play away from giving the ball back to Mahomes for a potential game-winning drive.

 However, Jones wanted to get pressure on Herbert so quickly that he lost outside contain, allowing the quarterback to scramble near the sideline for a 19-yard gain. Jones' mistakes, which he acknowledged after the game, led to a verbal confrontation between him and linebacker Drue Tranquill .

 As the Chiefs lost one-score game after one-score game -- finishing last season with a league-worst 1-9 record in such games -- the burden grew larger and larger for Jones: If he didn't impact the quarterback, his D-line teammates, other than Karlaftis, didn't provide much help.

 Against the Jacksonville Jaguars , Jones played 48 of 58 total snaps, the most of any defensive lineman. Jones showed that he was fatigued in the midst of the Jaguars' game-winning drive in the final minute, his final snap his most embarrassing. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence stumbled under center with the Jaguars at the 1-yard line trailing by four with just 30 seconds left. Jones, realizing he was going to be double-teamed again, didn't pursue Lawrence with maximum effort. A few seconds later, Jones watched Lawrence get up and scramble across the goal line for the winning touchdown.

 

 

 "This year, I plan to start high -- and go higher," said Jones, who led the Chiefs last season with seven sacks.

 

 Karlaftis struggled in the second half of the season, too, recording only one sack in his final seven games while he played through a nagging thumb injury. In November, during a four-game stretch, the Chiefs' defensive ends combined to get only one sack.

 "It was a humbling offseason," Karlaftis said. "It was the first offseason not coming off a Super Bowl [appearance]. I had to get my mind right. There was a month there that I was kind of looking at the man in the mirror and trying to figure out how I can help do my part so that what happened last year never happens again."

 Veach had a similar feeling. Most of the roster moves he made last season for the pass rush failed. Veach re-signed Charles Omenihu and Mike Danna , both of whom helped the Chiefs win two Super Bowls. Jerry Tillery and Janarius Robinson joined the team, too. None of them made significant contributions.

 The plan for the interior resulted in a bizarre outcome. The Chiefs didn't re-sign Derrick Nnadi after the 2024 season, choosing to retain Mike Pennel . But the Chiefs released Pennel after the preseason and then made a small trade with the New York Jets to acquire Nnadi. Once it was clear Nnadi wasn't an upgrade, the Chiefs in late October re-signed Pennel, who was released…

title: NFL fantasy outlook for Saints in 2026? Etienne, Johnson, rookie WRs
summary: With Alvin Kamara sidelined, fantasy managers are left to wonder who will pick up the carries for New Orleans.
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have almost made it to the start of the  2026 NFL regular season , but there have been a few bumps and bruises, especially when factoring in players' health and how that weighs in on their fantasy football outlooks.

 The Saints' short-term perspective is in flux, beginning with Week 1 at the Detroit Lions ( Sept. 13, 1 p.m. ET, Fox ) because of an injured running back room and injuries to rookies  Jordyn Tyson  (WR) and Oscar Delp  (TE).

 Here's what to look out for in fantasy for the next few weeks as the Saints' offense sorts its health issues out, while preparing for its first full season with quarterback Tyler Shough as the starter.

 
 Use of RBs in passing game 
 The Saints have three offensive players who can be relied on to take the majority of the snaps every week: Shough, running back  Travis Etienne Jr . and wide receiver Chris Olave .

 Etienne spent all of training camp with the first team and has experience shouldering most of the load after coming off a 260-carry season with the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2025. He will undoubtedly take the majority of the carries, especially with Alvin Kamara hurt due to a sprained MCL  he suffered on Aug. 18.

 

 The interesting thing will be how the Saints utilize their running backs in the passing game. That was Kamara's bread and butter for years. Etienne has that ability as well, even though he has never done it with the same volume Kamara had in his early NFL years.

 Saints offensive coordinator Doug Nussmeier said he feels some people had the perception Etienne was a receiver/running back earlier in his career because of his usage. He emphasized he sees an "elite running back" in him, despite his ability to catch passes as well.

 "Great instincts. He has great vision, great contact balance," Nussmeier said. "I just watched his tape in Jacksonville. There's a lot of things this guy does at an elite level, just a true tailback. So I think that maybe is a little bit of a misnomer about him. He does have good hands. Obviously he's been a big addition for us. We're really excited to see him go out and get to play."

 ESPN's Dan Graziano recently made a bold prediction that the Saints could have a top-10 rushing attack after finishing 28th in rushing yards per game last season. There's certainly reason to be optimistic about an improved unit after the Saints signed Etienne and David Edwards , who was one of the top offensive linemen on the market. 

 
 High-volume situations 
 With Tyson, the Saints' 2026 first-round pick, on short-term injured reserve , the team's passing offense presents an interesting challenge for fantasy managers. Devaughn Vele is the presumed No. 2 wide receiver in Tyson's absence, but there is no guarantee the No. 2 or No. 3 wideouts get a high volume of targets behind Olave.

 

 Tight end Juwan Johnson saw the second-most targets last season followed by Rashid Shaheed (who was traded mid-season), Kamara (who missed the final six games in 2025 with injury) and then Vele, who came on late in the season because of injuries. Vele had 25 receptions to Olave's 100.

 Johnson and the newly signed tight end Noah Fant  project be a big part of the passing game (Delp is injured), but it's Johnson who will probably receive the highest volume of targets. Both Johnson and Fant worked out with Shough in California this offseason, but Shough has trust in Johnson, who he was teammates with at Oregon in 2019.

 The running back position is tricky with so many injuries. Kamara has at least a month until he returns to the field, likely missing the first two games or more, depending on when he returns to practice.

 Running backs  Kendre Miller (unspecified injury) and Audric Estime (ankle) are also dealing with injuries. Estime could be a key fantasy pickup if he returns to practice by next week should Miller remain out.

 
 

 Saints players as late-round fliers 
 Wide receiver  Barion Brown , the Saints' sixth-round pick this year, might have flown under the radar nationally, but he quietly had a very good camp. That was enough to earn him a spot as one of the three starting running backs on the depth chart posted on the Saints official website this week.

 Brown was drafted with the reputation that he could be an NFL kick returner after returning six kickoffs for touchdowns at Kentucky and LSU. But he was given opportunities as a wide receiver early on in camp and took advantage. With Tyson out of the lineup for a while, that means Brown and fellow rookie Bryce Lance  (fourth-round pick) are going to get regular-season opportunities in the backfield.

 That training camp progress needs to translate to the regular season, but it's worth keeping an eye on one of the two rookies to see if the Saints utilize them in the regular rotation. Brown is listed above Lance as the top kick returner on the depth chart, and while he didn't return many kicks in training camp, that will most likely change come Week 1.

 "Those two guys have done an outstanding job of coming in and learning the system," Nussmeier said. "They've been productive players when they've been in the game. Obviously it's a new game when you get to the regular season versus the preseason, so they'll need to elevate their game again, but we're going to count on those guys to help us win."

title: Can Geno Smith rewrite his narrative in return to Jets?
summary: New York drafted the quarterback in 2013, and now he returns after a nine-year hiatus.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Brandon Marshall was only a few feet away from Geno Smith when the quarterback was sucker punched by a teammate. It was Aug. 11, 2015, a routine day in the  New York Jets ' locker room -- that is, until a simmering dispute over $600 exploded into violence.

 Smith was decked by linebacker IK Enemkpali, who delivered an uppercut that sent Smith into his locker and changed his career trajectory. In an instant, he went from QB1 to front-page headline.

 Marshall was stunned by what he witnessed that day. Over time, he has gained appreciation for the way Smith, now back for a second stint with the Jets, has responded.

 "You see what happened; something like that usually crushes guys -- it's over and it's done," the now-retired Marshall said. "You go to New York City, you lose it all and you're embarrassed, right? Your jaw is broken and you shut down and it's over.

 

 "But, no, he stayed the course. [He went from the role of] backup, backup, backup, backup, backup and -- boom: 'They wrote me off, I ain't write back though' -- one of the greatest moments over the past 50 years. His grandkids are going to see that when the NFL puts out the 50 best clips from the sideline."

 He was referring to Smith's viral comment from a postgame interview with ESPN's Lisa Salters after his 2022 Week 1 victory for the Seattle Seahawks -- his signature season in a career that has included more rises and falls than a volatile week on Wall Street.

 The 2022 AP Comeback Player of the Year is back with the team that drafted him in 2013, trying to stage yet another comeback after a disappointing season with the Las Vegas Raiders that raised some of the old questions about Smith, known as interception-prone.

 But those who know Smith say this is when he's at his best. Most athletes feed on doubt and criticism; for him, they're essential nourishment. His career started with a perceived slight -- he fell to the second round of the draft -- and he has collected similar receipts over the years.

 "He has this freaking, like, boss tenacity and leadership where guys are going to respect him," said Marshall, who lived with Smith for a few months before the 2015 season. "You can't push Geno over. That is needed in the locker room, especially today."

 

 

 THINGS DIDN'T END fondly in New York for Smith.

 He went 11-18 with 34 interceptions in two seasons as the Jets' starter, getting the job because of an injury (Mark Sanchez's season-ending shoulder surgery in the 2013 preseason) before losing it to Ryan Fitzpatrick because of his aforementioned broken jaw.

 Smith moved to the New York Giants in 2017 and became the guy who replaced Eli Manning for one game, ending Manning's iron man streak at 210 consecutive starts -- an infamous decision by Ben McAdoo that led to the coach's ouster.

 It's almost surreal that Smith is back where he began, trying to lift a franchise that hasn't enjoyed a winning season since he was injured and replaced by Fitzpatrick. There's something oddly karmic about Smith's return, something very Jets-ian. It would be a legacy-altering comeback if he can right the wrongs of his first incarnation.

 "That would be like a story in a movie, right?" Smith said. "[It would be] kind of like one of those superhero movies."

 The Jets have been looking for their Captain America since Joe Namath left them a half-century ago.

 When Smith takes the field for the season opener against the Tennessee Titans on Sept. 13 ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ), he will become their eighth different Week 1 starter in the past 11 years. His last season-opening start for the Jets was 2014 -- a 12-year separation. No quarterback in the Super Bowl era has had a longer gap between opening-day starts for a single franchise, according to ESPN Research.

 Digest this: He needs 332 passing yards to move past Zach Wilson for 10th place on the team's all-time list -- a factoid that could evoke a variety of emotions from Jets fans, impatiently waiting for a franchise quarterback.

 Can Smith, discarded by the 3-14 Raiders after a league-high 17 interceptions that landed them this year's No. 1 pick, pull off another comeback?

 "You've seen [ Sam Darnold ] come back and succeed elsewhere," said Tampa Bay Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles, Smith's second NFL coach. "You've seen [ Baker Mayfield ] come back and succeed elsewhere. You've seen quite a few guys. Daniel Jones has made a resurgence. Geno has played enough football. Maybe he's at the right place at the right time."

 Thing is, quarterbacks usually write their comeback stories after playing for the Jets -- see: Darnold and Smith 1.0 -- which means history is against him. Truth be told, it's against the entire franchise, which has the longest-running playoff drought (15 years) among the major sports in North America.

 

 If Smith, 35, is haunted by the past, he's not letting on.

 "I really cherish this opportunity," he said, knowing it could be his last chance as an undisputed starter.

 Smith seems earnest, as teammates and coaches have lauded his approach. He's "the alpha in the room," according to wide receiver Adonai Mitchell . Cornerback  Jarvis Brownlee Jr ., who, like Smith, was raised in the Miami area, called him a big brother. He said it's an honor to play with him. Several players, many of whom are 10 years his junior, said they grew up watching him.

 There's genuine respect for Smith's longevity, ability to overcome adversity and knowledge of the game. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich will be Smith's fifth different playcaller in the past four years, a head-spinning amount of instability. The upside is that he has seen just about everything from an X's and O's standpoint.

 "I always say the 'it' factor is the combination of a lot of confidence and genuine humility, and he's got both of those," Reich said.

 Smith wasn't always perceived this way. Early in his career, he experienced some "young" moments, including a missed team meeting in San Diego because he forgot about the three-hour time change.

 When Marshall arrived in 2015, he noticed in Smith a "raw ability to lead."

 "It wasn't fine-tuned when I got there" Marshall said. "He was still young and immature in some areas."

 Marshall shared his experiences, stressing how the starting QB must be an "executive figure" who commands respect from the locker room but also can maintain a good relationship with the coaches and front office.

 Smith said he leads through sound preparation and passion, not rah-rah speeches. He wants his teammates to "feel" him in the huddle. He has acknowledged personal growth throughout his career, once saying "[I] chose to let [the Enemkpali incident] fuel me to become a better man and a better player."

 His humbling journey has included backup jobs with the Giants (2017),  Los Angeles Chargers  (2018) and Seahawks (2019-24). He sat for three years in Seattle before he got his big shot.

 "The reason I fell in love with him was because I learned how he competed in a way that made him so unique," said former Seahawks and Raiders coach Pete Carroll, who named Smith to replace Russell Wilson in 2022. "Every single day he prepared like he was going to play the very next play. It wasn't like he moped or he took a break. I mean, he was on it always."

 
 

 A FEW YEARS ago, Smith and linebacker Demario Davis got into a deep conversation on the NFC team bus at the Pro Bowl. They had spent three seasons together with the Jets (2013-15), so there was common ground. They didn't talk much about football, though; it was about life and family. They never could've imagined they'd be teammates again.

 Davis, then a New Orleans Saints standout, was struck by how much Smith had matured from their days in New York.

 "You have to go through a certain amount of life to get that," said Davis, who, like Smith, returned to the Jets in 2026. "You can't just buy it."

 Smith has experienced a lot of life, good and bad. Once an aspiring artist, he…

title: An Eagles Q&A: Is Hurts acclimating? Will Lemon contribute?
summary: There is no shortage of storylines surrounding the Eagles as they ready for an intrigue-filled 2026 season.
full_text:
There is no shortage of storylines surrounding the Philadelphia Eagles as they ready for an intrigue-filled 2026 season.

 From Jalen Hurts and a new-look offense to expectations for rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon , there are plenty of questions for a team that finished 11-6, atop the NFC East before losing in the wild-card round to the 49ers.

 Let's examine a few key subplots with the opener versus the Washington Commanders on September 13 ( 4:25 p.m. ET, FOX ) rapidly approaching.

 

 

 How is Jalen Hurts acclimating to the new offense? 

 The feedback internally has been positive. For all the discussion about the number of coordinators Hurts has worked with, the scheme has largely remained the same in the Hurts/Nick Sirianni era. The West Coast style system being implemented by Sean Mannion , though, is a significant departure from how they've operated in the past. It's a heavy under-center operation. Hurts will often have his back to the defense when executing play-action instead of the more panoramic view from shotgun.

 Passing game coordinator Josh Grizzard described a timing-based aerial attack which requires Hurts to have consistent footwork and trust in his pass-catchers to be at the right place at the right time.

 "I think it's the commitment from the whole group," Grizzard said on what's impressed him most about the passing offense so far.

 "I think what you saw from the spring and where we're at right now, with everybody's understanding of the spacing of the field and the attention to fundamentals and details has really come a long way."

 There's going to be growing pains, no doubt. We witnessed some of that during the summer. Hurts threw double-digit interceptions during training camp -- much more than we're accustomed to seeing from him. Some of those fell on the receivers, some can be chalked up to a lack of synchronization in a new scheme, and some were on the QB. It's worth noting Hurts is making more over-the-middle throws in this offense and he got burned a handful of times while doing so.

 The real test for Hurts' commitment to this style of play will come during the regular season when the inevitable bumps in the road hit. The consensus to this point is he is bought in and fighting hard through the learning curve.  

 

 Is Makai Lemon ready to contribute? 

 Expectations should be tempered early.

 First-round picks always garner attention, and the interest was even higher around Lemon given A.J. Brown 's departure this offseason. But thoughts of him making a major impact out of the gate cooled as he missed minicamp and a good chunk of training camp with a hamstring injury.

 

 Lemon acknowledged it was the same hamstring giving him issues in the spring and summer. He raised some curiosity when he said he needed to be "more professional off the field" when speaking on the injury. Receivers coach Aaron Moorehead interpreted that as Lemon believing he needed to be "proactive with his pre-hab and his rehab and his stretching and all the things he needs to before practice, and come early.

 "I basically told him, 'Whatever Smitty [ DeVonta Smith ] does, you do.' And he's taken to that a little bit," Moorehead said.

 The coaches say Lemon attacked the mental part of the game with high intensity as he waited to get healthy. There's no substitution for on-field experience, however, and it will likely take a while for Lemon to fully get the timing of this offense down. He was only able to play in one preseason game and it didn't go particularly well, as he finished with three catches for three yards and had a pass glance off his hands that led to an interception.

 Lemon is expected to get playing time right off the bat but it's more likely that Smith and Dontayvion Wicks receive the bulk of targets while the rookie gets his footing.

 

 What has been the biggest under-the-radar development? 

 The emergence of offensive line depth.

 "If any of you would've given me a truth serum and said, 'What are you looking for in training camp?' it would be how our interior offensive line depth panned out," general manager Howie Roseman said recently.

 It was a natural place to have your eye trained. Left guard Landon Dickerson and center Cam Jurgens spent the bulk of last season battling through injuries that clearly impacted their play. And there wasn't much proven talent behind them entering the offseason.

 Second-year guard/centers Willie Lampkin and Drew Kendall shined during training camp in the preseason, however, and rookie guard Micah Morris , selected in the sixth round out of Georgia, impressed as well.

 The team's third-round pick, tackle Markel Bell , appears to have earned the role of swing tackle and could be the eventual replacement for Lane Johnson at right tackle.

 It's no secret the success of the Eagles has largely been predicated on their line play, and there's a sense of relief that the well appears full. It also reflects kindly on new offensive line coach Chris Kuper, who's had the daunting task of replacing one of the greats in Jeff Stoutland.

 

 Is the defense prepared to carry this team early if need be? 

 No question. This group has top-3 potential.

 There are All-Pro caliber players at every level, from defensive tackle Jalen Carter up front to linebacker Zack Baun in the middle to corners Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean in the back end. The addition of CB Riq Woolen , who has flashed his playmaking abilities a bunch this offseason since coming over from Seattle, could help make this one of the best secondaries in football.

 Not everything has gone right for the defense. Edge Jonathan Greenard , the Eagles' big offseason acquisition/ Jaelan Phillips replacement, injured his pec and missed all of training camp. They'll need Jalyx Hunt to keep the momentum from his red-hot summer going to help fuel the pass rush as Greenard heals and gets back up to speed.

 He'll have help from Nolan Smith Jr. and an interior line trio of Carter, Jordan Davis and Moro Ojomo that's as good as any in the NFL.

 Philly is loaded on the defensive side of the ball -- a luxury that, at a minimum, should keep the Eagles in every game.

title: How the 49ers, NFL made 'seamless' travel plan to Australia
summary: The 49ers touched down Thursday for their weeklong stay in Melbourne, Australia, to face the Rams. How did the team prepare for the trip?
full_text:
MELBOURNE, Australia -- By the time the San Francisco 49ers took off for Australia late Wednesday night Pacific Time, their Qantas Airbus A380 charter flight had four pilots, 22 cabin crew, one traveling charter manager and carried more than 95,000 pounds of human and material cargo. The payload included 220 passengers and their checked luggage, weighing in at an estimated 62,000 pounds, alongside 33,000 pounds of essential team equipment. 

 Perhaps more important than the cold weather gear (remember, winter in Australia just ended), helmets, shoulder pads and jerseys packed tightly into the aircraft was what wasn't on it: dirt.

 As the 49ers and the NFL collaborated over the past four months to move their football operation nearly 8,000 miles from the Bay Area to Melbourne, a unique challenge emerged of ensuring no California soil hitched a ride into one of the most isolated, ecologically guarded nations on the planet. Australia enforces some of the strictest biosecurity measures in the world. Introducing any sort of invasive species, insects or plant disease could lead to ecological and/or economic disaster, per the Australian government's Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. And while the cleaning process didn't need to be over the top -- the goal was to eliminate any large clumps of dirt or grass -- it added a layer of consideration as the Niners prepared for departure.

 "Australia is unlike any other market we've been to," said Joe Valentine, the NFL's director of international football operations & logistics. "This is a completely different operation. Being 8,000 miles away from home, 16-hour flight, 17-hour time difference, it's very, very different than the European setup or even the South American setup that we've become accustomed to. We've been way out more in front of this one because it is so different."

 

 Though an  exhibition was played between the Broncos and Chargers in Australia in 1999, the 49ers are the league's guinea pigs when it comes to operations and travel logistics for a regular-season game down under. San Francisco's 16-hour flight touched down in Melbourne on Friday morning Australian Eastern Standard Time (Thursday afternoon PT), giving the team a week to practice before its  season opener on Sept. 11 at 11:35 a.m. AEST (Sept. 10 at 5:35 p.m. PT). Meanwhile, the Rams are planning to arrive next Thursday and stay in Melbourne for roughly 24 hours.

 In this unchartered operational territory, some of the obstacles that 49ers and NFL officials pointed to include visa and passport acquisition; finding a plane big enough to carry the team comfortably; figuring out how to get through customs and security at the Melbourne airport; ensuring the practice facilities, hotel and stadiums were properly set up for an NFL team; and then how to break it all down and get back to California.

 The preparation started back in March, Valentine said, when the NFL asked the Rams and 49ers to send any items they would want but didn't immediately need for Week 1 to a cargo ship in New York. That cargo ship also carried an additional 60,000 pounds of equipment from the league, including goal posts, Gatorade products and coolers, field equipment (chains, pylons, etc.), practice site equipment and medical gear.

 The ship departed on April 15 and arrived a little more than two weeks ago. And lest anyone believe Australia didn't take its biosecurity efforts seriously, customs agents denied San Francisco's supply of protein powder from entering the country.

 Under normal circumstances, every NFL team is responsible for makings its own travel arrangements. But with such a long flight and so much to take on it, the league office played a large role in helping the 49ers figure out a flight plan.

 In search of a plane that would provide plenty of space for a football team, the league worked with Qantas to secure one of its 10 Airbus A380s. Those planes have 84 lie-flat seats (14 first class plus 70 business) and 60 premium economy seats out of the roughly 400 total seats. As per usual, the Niners gave players the most desirable seats so they could get their required sleep. Qantas even went so far as to provide some customized pajamas to help the cause.

 Because those planes are so large, they can't simply fly out of any airport whenever the teams want. The Niners said they evaluated all their options and decided late in the spring to do the full week trip.

 "Obviously, that comes with a lot of planning and process to get two very large airplanes off the ground and make sure they land in Melbourne in the right fashion," said Charlotte Offord, the general manager of NFL Australia and New Zealand. "There's a few logistics there."

 

 For domestic games, teams generally fly into the opposing city and never set foot in the terminal. Instead, they simply go through security either at the team facility before traveling to the airport or on the tarmac. When arriving in Australia, it was not quite as straightforward, though the league believes it created something as close to normal as possible.

 "There's a lot of steps to it," Valentine said. "We want it to be seamless; we want it to be efficient."

 Before the Niners boarded their plane, they had to navigate a strenuous monthlong passport and visa distribution process. The team hosted the Department of State for three days at its Santa Clara facility and worked with the San Francisco Passport agency to ensure everyone had one in time before departure.

 Visa acquisition was a far more arduous process that required attention nearly every day of the final month before departure. Players and coaches needed a Subclass 408 working visa, which requires more information and effort to acquire than the ETA digital travel permit that behind-the-scenes folks needed.

 The entire process became more difficult when it collided with the reality of building a final 53-man NFL roster and practice squad. As late as Tuesday afternoon, the Niners were still finalizing the visa process, which left one practice squad signee asking his parents to overnight his passport from his house.

 "I've never [had to] ask a potential practice squader, 'Do you have a passport?'" general manager John Lynch said. "Those are questions we have to ask now ... there's a lot of little logistics like that that are complicated by this. You know, we're embracing it. We're having a plan for everything and we're getting it done."

 After completing the longest flight any NFL team has ever taken for a regular-season game, the 49ers will spend the rest of the day recovering from the flight at their team hotel. An advance crew of dieticians, security, information technology, logistics, equipment, video and kitchen staff arrived early to convert the hotel into the team's Melbourne headquarters.

 When the 49ers practice Saturday, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at AAMI Park, they'll walk into the home of the Melbourne Storm (four-time winner of the National Rugby League) and two A-League soccer teams (Melbourne Victory FC and Melbourne City FC). The NFL helped tweak the stadium's facilities to replicate the team's recovery environment in Santa Clara, adding hot and cold tubs, medical gear and training equipment.

 The 49ers also consulted multiple rugby teams, European soccer teams and a couple of Australian rules football clubs for local support on where to find massage therapists and different health clubs. They even talked to Stanford football, which traveled to Sydney in 2017 for a game against Rice . For game day, the league sourced local vendors to create the specs of an NFL locker room at the Melbourne Cricket Grounds and expand coaches booths to fit the staff size of the teams.

 

 "In every stadium we go through, we're knocking down walls and we're plumbing and we're adding showers and toilets and cold tubs and hot tubs if they don't have them," said Jon Barker, the NFL's senior vice president and global head of major…
